x: What is 3D printing? · 3D Printing Compendium Part 1 · Foundations What is 3D printing? 3D printing builds objects by adding material one thin layer at a time, straight from a digital file. This page gives you the complete mental map: how it differs from other ways of making things, the processes, the workflow, the history, the vocabulary and what to realistically expect. Beginner ⏱ 30 min read What you will learn How additive, subtractive and formative manufacturing differ, and why each exists. The seven official process families and where desktop printers fit. The five-stage workflow every print follows, from idea to finished part. Why printed parts have layer lines, how X/Y/Z coordinates work, and the words you will hear every day. What 3D printing is great at, what it is bad at, and a fair picture of time, money and learning curve. 🔰 The big idea: three ways to make a thing Every manufactured object, from a spoon to a jet engine bracket, was made by one of three broad strategies. Understanding them makes it obvious why 3D printing is exciting, and also why it has not replaced everything else. Figure 1. Subtractive methods carve a part out of a solid block, formative methods squeeze or pour material into a mold, and additive methods build the part from nothing, so material is placed only where it is needed. Question Subtractive Formative Additive (3D printing) Material waste High chips and offcuts Low–medium sprues, flash Low mostly supports and purge Up-front tooling Fixtures, cutters Molds: very costly None Cost of the 1st part Medium Very high Low Cost of the 10,000th part Medium Very low About the same as the first Geometric freedom Limited by tool access Limited by mold release Internal channels, lattices, organic shapes Surface finish Excellent Excellent Visible layers unless finished Part strength Isotropic, from solid stock Isotropic Direction-dependent (weaker between layers) Best for Precise metal parts, flat sheets Mass production One-offs, prototypes, custom and complex parts Why "additive" is a big deal With subtractive and formative methods, complexity costs money: more axes, more cutters, more mold slides. In additive manufacturing the cost is driven mainly by volume and print time , not by shape. A hollow, curved, internally ribbed part can cost less than a solid block. That is the one idea to remember. Four practical strengths 🧩 Complexity is free Hollow shapes, channels, lattices and organic curves cost no more than simple boxes. ⚡ No tooling From file to part with no mold, jig or cutter set. Ideal for one-offs and small runs. 🔁 Fast iteration Change a number in the model and have a new version the same day, often the same afternoon. 🎯 Customization Every part can be different: a hand brace for one person, a bracket for one weird machine. 🔰 The seven process families "3D printing" is a nickname. The formal term is additive manufacturing (AM) , and the international standard ISO/ASTM 52900 sorts all additive methods into seven categories based on how layers are created and bonded. Nearly everything you will do at home or in a classroom is the first category (material extrusion), with resin vat printing a distant second. The others live in industry and service bureaus, but you should know they exist because they appear in the news, in job listings and in the parts you buy. Figure 2. The seven ISO/ASTM 52900 categories. Home and classroom printers are almost always category 1 (orange) or category 2 (purple). Family Typical materials Who uses it Where it is covered here Material extrusion PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, nylon, TPU, composites Hobbyists, schools, engineers, small factories The core of this compendium Vat photopolymerization Photopolymer resins Miniatures, jewelry, dental, detailed prototypes Printing processes Powder bed fusion Nylon powders, metals Service bureaus, aerospace, production of small parts Printing processes Material jetting Multi-color photopolymers Product design, medical models Printing processes Binder jetting Metal, sand, ceramic, full-color powder Foundries, architecture models Printing processes Directed energy deposition Metal wire or powder Large metal repair and structures Printing processes Sheet lamination Paper, plastic or metal foil Niche: models, ultrasonic metal parts Mentioned for completeness 🔰 The complete workflow: idea → part No matter which printer you own, every successful print follows the same five stages. When something goes wrong later in this course, the first question is always " which stage did the problem enter? " Knowing the pipeline makes troubleshooting far easier. Figure 3. The five-stage pipeline. Each stage hands a specific file or object to the next, and the dashed loop is where most of the learning happens. Stage 1 · Idea and requirements Every good part starts with a question: what must it do? A phone stand only needs to hold weight and look decent. A bracket near a hot motor must survive temperature. A hinge must flex thousands of times. Writing down three things (size, load, environment) before you open any software prevents most disappointment and tells you which material to choose later. See the materials overview when you reach that question. Stage 2 · The 3D model A printer cannot print a picture; it needs a solid, watertight 3D shape . You get one in three ways: Download from a repository such as MakerWorld, Printables or Thingiverse. The fastest way to start, and the way almost everyone begins. Design in CAD (computer-aided design) software. Beginners use browser tools like Tinkercad; engineers use parametric tools like Fusion, Onshape or FreeCAD. See CAD & modeling software . Scan a real object with photogrammetry or a 3D scanner, then clean the mesh. See file formats & mesh repair . The model is exported as a mesh file (usually STL or 3MF ). x: Printing processes compared · 3D Printing Compendium Part 1 · Foundations Printing processes compared Melting plastic through a nozzle is only one way to build in layers. This page tours every major process, shows how each one works, compares them on detail, strength, cost, safety and post-processing, and helps you choose the right one for a given part. Beginner Intermediate depth ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn How FDM, resin, powder-bed, jetting, binder and metal processes actually create a layer. Which process delivers fine detail, which delivers strength, and which delivers low cost. What post-processing and safety each process demands in practice. How to choose a process for a given part with a simple decision tree. How hybrid workflows combine processes (for example, print a master, then cast it). 🔰 The tour at a glance Before the detail, here is the map. If you read the previous page , you know that the standards body groups additive manufacturing into seven families. In daily life those families split into many commercial names. The cards below link each name to its family and to the audience that usually buys it. 🧵 FDM / FFF Melted filament extruded from a nozzle. The default for hobby, education and functional prototyping. 💧 Resin: SLA · MSLA · DLP Light cures liquid photopolymer. Best fine detail on small parts; messier workflow. 🏜️ SLS · MJF Fusing nylon powder. No supports, strong parts, mostly ordered from services or run in small workshops. 🎨 PolyJet / material jetting Inkjet-style droplets of resin: multi-color, multi-material, very smooth. Costly. 🪨 Binder jetting Glue printed into powder. Full-color models, sand cores for casting, metal via sintering. ⚙️ Metal: LPBF · DMLS · EBM · DED Lasers or electron beams fuse metal powder or wire. Industrial, expensive, and remarkable. 🔩 Bound-metal filament Metal powder in plastic is printed on an FDM machine, then debound and sintered in a furnace. 🚀 CLIP · volumetric Continuous or all-at-once resin processes that avoid visible layers. Mostly industrial or research. 🏗️ Pellet · concrete · bio Large-format plastic from pellets, building-scale concrete and cell-laden bioinks. 🔰 FDM / FFF: extrusion of thermoplastic Fused deposition modeling (FDM) , also called fused filament fabrication (FFF) , is the process behind almost every consumer printer you will meet. A thermoplastic strand (filament) is pushed into a heated nozzle, melts, and is laid down as a thin bead that fuses to the layer below and solidifies within a fraction of a second. The toolhead traces each layer's outline and fills the interior; then the nozzle rises one layer height and repeats. Figure 1. The FDM chain from spool to part. The "cold end" (extruder, heat sink) must stay cool so filament stays rigid until it reaches the "hot end". More in Anatomy of an FDM printer . 🔰 Why FDM dominates hobby printing Cost: capable machines are available from a few hundred dollars; filament is roughly US$15–30 per kilogram for common types. Material range: PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, nylon, polycarbonate, TPU, composites with carbon or glass fiber, and many specialty types (see Materials overview ). Simple workflow: there is no liquid, no powder and no curing station. Remove the part, remove supports and you are done. Size: build volumes of 200–350 mm per side are standard and much larger machines exist. Strength: functional parts in engineering plastics are realistic. 🔧 Limits you should know Resolution: the nozzle diameter sets the smallest feature; with a 0.4 mm nozzle, features thinner than roughly 0.4–0.8 mm are unreliable. Layer lines are visible and the surface is textured unless you finish it. Anisotropy: parts are weaker across layers than along them. Overhangs need supports or careful design; see Supports, bridges & overhangs . FDM versus FFF "FDM" is a trademark of Stratasys. "FFF" is the generic, community-created term with the same meaning. In practice, people use them interchangeably, and so does this compendium. 🔰 Resin printing: SLA, MSLA and DLP In vat photopolymerization , the "ink" is a liquid photopolymer: a resin whose molecules link into a solid when exposed to the right wavelength of light (typically UV around 365–405 nm). The build plate dips into a vat of resin, light cures one layer, the plate lifts, fresh resin flows in, and the next layer is exposed. Three light-delivery methods exist: Method How the layer is drawn Strengths Weaknesses SLA (laser) A UV laser and scanning mirrors trace the layer point by point Very smooth, accurate large parts, mature industrial machines Slower for filling large areas; more expensive optics DLP A projector flashes the entire layer image at once Fast; pixel size is fixed by the projector Detail drops as the build area grows; projector lamp or LED aging MSLA (LCD) A UV LED array shines through a monochrome LCD that masks the layer Low-cost, high resolution on small areas, the common desktop type LCD screens wear out and are consumables; light uniformity varies Figure 2. Cross-section of an MSLA vat. Light only passes where the LCD is transparent (the white gap under the part); everywhere else the black pixels block it. After each exposure the plate lifts, peeling the new layer off the film, and resin flows back under the part. 🔰 What the layer cycle looks like Lower the plate The plate descends until the part sits one layer height above the film. Expose The LCD shows the slice and the LEDs flash for a few seconds (bottom layers get much longer exposures so the part sticks to the plate). Peel The plate lifts; the freshly cured layer has to separate from the film. Peeling creates suction and force that can pull parts off the plate or tear thin features. Rest and refill Resin flows back under the part. Viscous resins need a short pause. Repeat Often several hundred to several thousand layers at 0.03–0.1 mm each. 🔧 Resolution and accuracy On an MSLA printer the XY resolution is set by the pixel pitch of the screen (commonly aroun

x: Anatomy of an FDM printer · 3D Printing Compendium Part 1 · Foundations Anatomy of an FDM printer A filament printer looks like a box with a moving head, but every part in it has a job, a failure mode and a trade-off. This page takes the machine apart on paper: frame, motion systems, hotend, extruder, nozzle, bed, electronics, sensors and the software tricks that make modern printers fast. Beginner Intermediate Some advanced detail ⏱ 45 min read What you will learn The name and purpose of every major subsystem of an FDM printer. How Cartesian, CoreXY, delta, IDEX and tool-changer designs differ in speed, quality and cost. What is inside a hotend, why the heat break matters, and how extruders grip filament. Which nozzle material, nozzle size and build surface suit which job. How bed probing, input shaping and sensors keep prints reliable at high speed. How automatic multi-material systems feed filament to the toolhead. 🔰 The nine subsystems Strip away the branding and every FDM printer has the same nine subsystems. Learning to see them lets you diagnose problems ("is this a motion problem or a melt problem?") and compare machines without being distracted by marketing. The labeled drawing below shows a typical enclosed machine with a moving bed on the Z axis. Figure 1. Front view of a typical enclosed FDM printer. Real machines differ in layout (many hide the extruder inside the toolhead, some move the bed in Y instead of Z) but the same subsystems are always present. Subsystem Main parts Its job Typical failure signs Frame Aluminum extrusion, steel or cast panels, feet Hold everything square and rigid Ringing, layer shifts, wobble on a shaky table Motion Steppers, belts, rails/rods, leadscrews, pulleys Place the nozzle at exact X/Y/Z positions Dimensional errors, banding, grinding noise Hotend Heat sink, heat break, heater, thermistor, nozzle Melt filament and shape the bead Clogs, heat creep, under-extrusion, oozing Extruder Motor, gears, idler/pressure arm Push filament at a precise rate Skipped steps, clicking, ground filament Bed Heater, sensor, build plate, leveling Hold the first layer flat and hot Warping, poor adhesion, uneven first layer Electronics Mainboard, drivers, PSU, wiring, screen Run firmware and power everything Resets, layer shifts, thermal faults Sensors Thermistors, probes, filament sensors, accelerometer Close the loop on temperature, position and feed False runout alarms, failed leveling Cooling Part fan, hotend fan, aux/chamber fans Solidify plastic quickly, protect the heat sink Drooping overhangs, heat creep Enclosure Panels, door, lid, filters Hold heat, block drafts, contain fumes Warping, heat-soaked extruder, noise Read a machine in 60 seconds When you look at a new printer, ask three questions: what moves (the bed, the head, or both?), how does filament reach the nozzle (direct drive or Bowden?), and how is the first layer measured (manual, inductive probe, strain, eddy current, load cell?). These three answers predict most of its speed, noise and day-to-day maintenance. 🔰 Frame, motion and the rigidity budget The frame is boring and critical. A printer is a machine that places a hot nozzle with a precision of tenths of a millimeter while accelerating it at several meters per second squared. Every bit of flex in the frame becomes a visible ripple in the wall. That is why premium machines use thick castings or steel sheet, why cheap ones wobble when you tap the top, and why where you put the printer matters almost as much as which one you buy (see Safety & workspace ). 🧱 Aluminum extrusion T-slot profiles bolted together. Cheap, adjustable and easy to repair; stiffness depends on corner joints and bracing. 🔩 Sheet steel and castings Stamped panels or die-cast parts. Heavier, stiffer and quieter; used in many enclosed machines. 🔧 Open or kit frames Fewer parts and more flex. Great for learning and repair, less good at high acceleration. Stepper motors, drivers and microstepping Almost every axis is moved by a stepper motor : a motor that turns in discrete steps (typically 200 per revolution, 1.8° each). A driver chip on the mainboard energizes the coils in sequence and can split each full step into 16, 32 or more microsteps for smoother motion. Modern silent drivers (the TMC family is the best known) also sense the motor current and can detect a stalled motor, which is how some printers do sensorless homing . Resolution is not accuracy. A belt axis with a 20-tooth pulley and a 2 mm belt pitch moves 40 mm per revolution, so one full step is 0.2 mm and one microstep (at 16×) is about 12.5 µm in theory. What you actually get depends on belt stretch, pulley fit and frame flex. Belts, leadscrews, rods and linear rails Belts (X and Y) Toothed GT2 belts are light and fast but stretch slightly under load. Keep them tensioned, never over-tight, and replace them when teeth wear or fiber shows. Leadscrews (usually Z) A threaded rod turns the rotation into slow, strong vertical lift with fine resolution. Most Z axes use leadscrews so the bed cannot drift down when power is off. Smooth rods + bushings Hardened steel rods with linear bearings or bushings. Inexpensive and quiet when well aligned; more friction and sag than rails. Linear rails (guide rails) Profiled rails with recirculating ball carriages. Stiffer, more precise and long-lasting, at higher cost and with more demanding alignment. Why Z is different X and Y need speed, so they use belts. Z needs strength and fine steps (layer heights are 0.08–0.32 mm), so it uses screws. Some machines drive Z with a belt and counterweights or with multiple synchronized screws to keep a heavy bed level. ⚙️ Kinematics: who moves where Kinematics is the arrangement that decides which part moves in which axis. It is the single biggest design choice in a printer, because it sets how much mass must be accelerated and therefore how fast the machine can print before quality falls apart. Figure 2. x: Your first print · 3D Printing Compendium Part 1 · Foundations Your first print A calm, step-by-step walkthrough from the closed box to a finished part on the plate. The steps apply to almost any filament printer; where a machine-specific detail matters, you will see a short note. By the end you will know what good looks like, what to do when it does not, and what to print next. Beginner ⏱ 40 min read 🖨 first job: about 1–2 hours What you will learn How to unbox, inspect, place and power up a printer safely. How to load filament correctly and why a clean cut matters. Which model to print first and why, and how to slice it with sensible defaults. How to read the first layer, the best predictor of success. How to remove, clean and store the result, and which ten prints to do next. Using a Bambu Lab printer? Read this page for the concepts, then follow the machine-specific walkthrough in Setup and first print . Bambu machines automate several steps below (calibration, leveling and filament recognition), so you will mostly watch rather than adjust. 🔰 The mental model: what is happening Before touching the machine, it helps to know what the machine is going to do. A 3D print is a loop of instruction, motion, melting and feedback. You provide a model; software turns it into thousands of tiny moves; the printer follows them while checking its temperatures and positions. Figure 1. A print is a pipeline: your file becomes G-code, the printer executes it, and sensors keep the loop honest. Three ingredients decide success Almost every first-print failure comes from one of three things: the nozzle is the wrong distance from the plate (first layer), the filament is wet or not flowing (extrusion), or the part is not stuck down or not sliced sensibly (adhesion and orientation). Keep these in mind and the troubleshooting section at the end will read like common sense. 📦 Step 1: unboxing and inspection Keep the box and the packing materials until the machine has printed successfully; you will need them if you must return it. Unpack on a clear table and take your time. Many "broken" printers are simply still locked for transport. Figure 2. Typical inspection points. Every manufacturer locks different parts for transport, so always read the quick-start card that came in the box. Voltage and mains Some printers ship with a mains voltage selector on the back. Check it matches your wall supply before the first power-on, and use the supplied or a certified cable in a properly grounded outlet. See Safety & workspace for outlet, surge and fire safety. 📍 Step 2: placement Where a printer lives shapes how often you will use it. A good location is stable, ventilated, near a power outlet and not in a bedroom or somewhere you would not smell a problem. Leave space for the door, the lid and the filament spool. Figure 3. Plan view of a sensible printer spot. Distances are rules of thumb; follow the manual for the exact clearance of your machine. Table or shelf is level and does not wobble when you push it. There is a power outlet within cable reach; avoid extension cables and adapters for heated machines. Room is ventilated and has a working smoke detector. Nothing flammable sits next to or above the printer. Filament has a dry, dust-free place to wait. 🔌 Step 3: first power-up and calibration On first start most printers walk you through a series of self-tests. Do not skip them. They teach the machine its own geometry and tune it for vibration. Figure 4. What a typical first start-up does. If your printer has an auto-calibration button, run it once after unpacking and any time you move the machine. Connect and update. Join Wi-Fi or insert an SD/USB stick if needed, and install the firmware update. Updates fix real bugs and safety issues. Home the machine. It moves each axis until it finds its limit. Stand clear and listen for grinding or knocking; if you hear it, stop and re-check transit locks. Run vibration and bed calibration. These can take several minutes; the head moves and the bed heats. Let it finish; do not touch the plate while it probes. Check the Z offset. If the printer asks for a first-layer calibration, accept it. See the first-layer section below for what to look for. Manual leveling If your printer is a basic model with adjustable bed screws, level it hot: heat the bed to printing temperature, then use the paper test at each corner. You want light drag on a sheet of copy paper. Re-check after the first few prints because springs settle. 🧵 Step 4: loading filament The loading procedure differs slightly between printers, but the idea is identical: heat the nozzle, push filament until it flows, and stop when the plastic extrudes cleanly. Figure 5. The filament path. A clean angled cut and a free-spinning spool prevent most loading problems. Heat means burns The nozzle reaches 200 °C or more. Never reach into the print area to guide filament with the nozzle hot unless the manual says it is safe; use pliers or wait for it to cool. Start with PLA PLA is the right first material: low temperature (about 190–220 °C), minimal warping, little odor, and tolerant of imperfect settings. Move to PETG, ABS and engineering materials later; see the materials section of this compendium. 🎯 Step 5: choose a first model Your first print should be small, flat on the bottom, forgiving, and tell you something. Avoid your dream project; you will be learning the machine at the same time. Three classic candidates exist, and each teaches something different. Figure 6. Pick one of these three. The cube verifies basics, the boat stress-tests everything, and a practical part shows what printing is for. Why not start big? A large print is a long bet: any early flaw ruins hours of work and wastes filament. A small print gives you a result and a lesson in under an hour. x: Safety & workspace · 3D Printing Compendium Part 1 · Foundations Safety & workspace A 3D printer is a small, hot, moving, electrically powered machine that makes particles and vapors. None of that is a reason to be afraid of it; it is a reason to set it up sensibly. This page covers the real hazards, how big they actually are, and the practical habits that keep them small. Beginner Practical ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn The main hazards of FDM and resin printing and how to rank them. How fire risk arises and the layered defences that reduce it. What fumes and ultrafine particles are, which materials emit more, and how ventilation and filtration help. How to handle resin and chemicals safely. How to lay out a workspace, choose a stable bench and plan power and storage. What to buy for a beginner tool kit, and what to do in an emergency. Calm, evidence-based, not alarmist Millions of people print at home without incident. The sensible approach is the same as for a kitchen or a workshop: know the main hazards, apply a few inexpensive controls, and do not rely on a single safeguard. This page gives general guidance, not legal, medical or insurance advice; the manufacturer's manual and your local rules always take precedence. 🔰 The hazard map Hazards cluster in a few places on the machine. Seeing them on a drawing makes the list below easier to remember. Figure 1. The five hazard groups. Burn and cut injuries are common and minor; fire is uncommon but severe; fumes are chronic and controllable. Hazard How likely How severe Main control Burns Common Minor to moderate Let it cool; use tools; keep hands out while hot. Cuts Common Minor Cut away from the body; sharp tools used on a stable surface. Pinching / entanglement Occasional Minor Power off before reaching in; tie hair; no loose sleeves. Fire Rare High Safeguards on; smoke detector; no modified firmware limits; supervision. Electric shock Rare High Grounded outlet; no opened PSU; unplug before repair. Fumes / particles Continuous Low per print Material choice, ventilation, enclosure and filtration. Resin chemicals Frequent Skin sensitization Gloves, ventilation, containment, correct disposal. 🔥 Burns and moving parts The nozzle runs at 200–300 °C and the bed at 40–110 °C depending on the material; many chamber-heated machines keep the whole interior warm. A bare-skin touch of the nozzle causes a burn within a fraction of a second, and molten plastic sticks to skin and makes it worse. The bed stays hot for several minutes after the end of a print. Treat everything inside the printer as hot until the display says otherwise. Use pliers or tweezers for stray strands, never your fingers near the nozzle. When removing parts from a hot bed, wait or wear heat-resistant gloves. Treat a burn with cool running water straight away, for at least 20 minutes (British and Australian Red Cross guidance), and seek medical help for blisters or large areas. Moving parts Gantries, belts, fans and extruder gears move with enough force to pinch or pull. Printers are usually slow enough that injuries are minor, but fast machines accelerate hard. Good habits: power off before reaching in for maintenance; tie back long hair; avoid loose sleeves and jewellery near belts; and keep fingers out of the door opening during motion. Many enclosed printers pause when the door opens; do not rely on this as the only protection. Never bypass interlocks If your machine has a door sensor or a protective cover, leave it enabled. Taping over a door switch to keep printing with the door open removes a safeguard that was designed with the manufacturer's testing in mind. ⚡ Electrical safety A printer draws more power than most desk electronics: a heated bed alone can use several hundred watts, and fast machines peak above 1 kW. That current flows through connectors and thin wires that move with the toolhead and bed, which fatigue over time. Outlet: use a properly grounded wall outlet. Avoid long daisy chains of power strips and cheap adapters; use a quality strip rated for the load if you must. Mains voltage switch: where present, set it before power-up. PSU and mainboard: never open the power supply with the cable connected. Capacitors store charge after unplugging. Connectors: inspect heater and bed connectors for discolouration, melting or loose pins every few months. A hot, browned connector is a warning that must be fixed before the next print. Modifications: if you replace a heater, thermistor or board, use parts rated for the current and match the firmware settings. Many fire incidents trace back to a mismatched upgrade. Residual current device (RCD / GFCI): workshop circuits with a protective breaker reduce shock risk. Many homes already have one. Power loss and UPS Mid-print power loss happens. Many modern printers can resume from the last layer. A UPS (uninterruptible power supply) can keep a printer running through short outages but must be sized for the machine's peak draw, including the bed heater; small desktop UPS units are often too small and can overload. If you want resume protection, check the printer's features before buying a UPS. 🧯 Fire risk and defense in depth Fire is the rare but serious hazard, so it deserves layered defences. Typical causes are a failed or disabled thermal runaway protection, a loose heater connector that overheats, incorrect modification, dust and filament debris near hot parts, and a flammable object left near the machine. Single failures happen; the aim is to make sure no single failure becomes a fire. Figure 2. Fire safety works as concentric layers. Outer layers catch what inner layers miss. Smoke detector (preferably photoelectric) in the room where the printer sits, tested monthly. Extinguisher rated for electrical fires (CO₂ or dry-powder ABC) within reach of the exit, not above the printer. Thermal runaway protection is enabled in the firmware; never flash firmware with protections removed. Heater, bed and PSU connectors inspe

x: Choosing a printer · 3D Printing Compendium Part 1 · Foundations Choosing a printer The best printer is the one that fits your parts, your space, your patience and your budget. This guide turns that into a method: define the need, pick a machine category, look past the marketing numbers, then count the real cost over a year. Beginner ⏱ 30 min read Goal of this page You will be able to write down what you need from a printer, map it to a machine type, compare candidates on the specs that actually matter, and estimate the first-year cost honestly. Brand names appear only as examples; specifications and prices change quickly, so check current sources before buying. 🎯 Start with the need, not the machine Most regrets come from buying for a hypothetical use. Before you read a single spec sheet, answer six questions honestly. Write the answers down; they will filter the market far more effectively than any review. 1 · What will you print? Display models and figurines, functional brackets and enclosures, tools and jigs, cosplay, miniatures, prototypes? Each leans toward a different process and size. 2 · How big are the parts? Measure your biggest wish-list part. Most useful parts fit in a 250 mm cube; helmets, furniture parts and large props do not, but they can be split and glued. 3 · Which materials? PLA and PETG are easy on any machine. ABS, ASA, nylon and carbon-fiber blends need a heated, enclosed chamber and a hardened nozzle. Flexible TPU wants a good direct-drive extruder. 4 · How many colors? Single-color with painting, a few colors via a multi-material system, or many colors with little waste? Color changes cost time and filament. 5 · How much tinkering? Do you want to press print and get a result, or do you enjoy tuning, repairing and upgrading? Honest answers prevent frustration either way. 6 · Where will it live? Noise, fumes, space, power and neighbors matter. See Safety & workspace before you commit to a spot. Figure 1. A simplified decision tree. It points to a category, not a model. Treat the answer as a shortlist starting point and read the sections below to refine it. 🗂 The main printer categories Almost every consumer printer falls into one of six families. Here is what each is good at, and what it costs you in other ways. Price bands are rough and change with the market. Figure 2. The six families in outline. Real machines differ in detail, but this structure explains most of the trade-offs in speed, noise, material choice and price. Category Strengths Trade-offs Typical price band* Entry bedslinger Cheapest; huge community; easy to repair and upgrade Slower for good quality; usually open; more tuning $ low Enclosed CoreXY Fast, quiet-ish, engineering materials, strong defaults Heavier, costlier; some designs are tied to one ecosystem $$ mid Multi-material Multi-color, soluble or breakaway supports, auto spool change Waste (purge), more complexity, more consumables $$ mid Large format Big parts in one piece; fewer joins Slow, space-hungry, warps more, higher power draw $$$ high Resin (MSLA) Fine detail, smooth surfaces, small parts Messy, toxic liquid, post-processing, small volume $ – $$ IDEX / toolchanger Mirror/duplicate mode, many materials, high throughput Calibration of offsets, price, learning curve $$$ high *Bands are relative and market-dependent. Compare current prices yourself; budget kits and premium machines overlap. Reading the categories in practice Entry bedslingers are where the hobby grew up. The bed slides back and forth under the nozzle, which is simple and cheap but limits acceleration because the mass of the bed (and the print on it) must change direction. They teach you a lot because they reward understanding: levelling, tuning, retraction and cooling all matter. If you enjoy the machine as a project, this is a fine place to start. If you only want parts, the time you spend tuning may feel like a tax. Enclosed CoreXY machines keep the bed moving only up and down while a light toolhead moves in X and Y. That allows high acceleration with good quality, and the enclosure stabilizes temperature, reduces drafts and contains fumes and noise. For most people who want to print functional parts reliably, this is the sweet spot. See the kinematics section for how the belts work. Multi-material machines add automatic filament switching, a second nozzle or both. They unlock multi-color models, dissolvable supports and mixed material parts, at the cost of purge waste and more things that can jam. We look at them in their own section below. Large-format printers are for objects that do not split well: helmets, enclosures, furniture. Remember that doubling a part's length multiplies its print time by far more than two, and that big flat parts in warp-prone materials fight you. Resin printers deliver detail that filament cannot match: miniatures, jewellery masters, dental-style models, fine mechanical parts. The price is a chemical workflow. Read Printing processes and the resin safety section first. IDEX and toolchanger systems have two or more independent heads. IDEX (independent dual extruders) can print two copies at once in mirror or duplicate mode, which doubles throughput for identical parts, or use two materials. Toolchangers switch between many heads for multi-color printing with very little waste. They are powerful but more expensive and need careful offset calibration. 📏 Specs that matter, and specs that mostly do not Spec sheets are written to sell. A few numbers carry real information; many are noise. Use the table as a filter. Specs worth comparing Build volume that matches your biggest regular part, with a little margin. Maximum nozzle and bed temperatures : determine which materials are possible. Enclosure and chamber heating : decide whether ABS, ASA and nylon are realistic. Extruder type : direct drive handles flexible filament far better. Nozzle material and swap-ability : hardened nozzles for abrasive filament. Bed surface and levelling : automati

x: Filament overview & comparison · 3D Printing Compendium Part 2 · Materials Filament overview & comparison Learn what is actually on the spool, why plastics behave the way they do when heated and cooled, and how to pick the right material from a field of dozens, using charts, ladders and one decision flowchart. Beginner → Advanced ⏱ 35 min read What you will learn What filament is: diameter, tolerance, spool, color, and additives. The polymer science that explains almost every printing rule: amorphous vs semi-crystalline, glass transition, shrinkage, moisture and layer bonding. A master comparison of about 27 materials, with temperatures, enclosure needs, strength, heat resistance, price and printability. How to choose a material with a flowchart, and when you need a hardened nozzle. 🔰 What filament actually is Filament is thermoplastic that has been melted, extruded through a precise die, cooled, and wound onto a spool as a long, thin, round “wire”. An FDM (fused deposition modeling, also called FFF) printer pulls it off the spool, pushes it into a heated nozzle, melts it, and lays it down line by line and layer by layer. Because the plastic is a thermoplastic , it softens when heated and hardens when cooled, again and again. That is the only reason the process works, and it is also why a printed part can soften in a hot car. Almost all consumer printers, including the Bambu Lab X2D, use filament with a nominal diameter of 1.75 mm . A second standard, 2.85 mm (often called “3 mm”), exists for a few older or industrial machines. The two are not interchangeable, so always check what your printer accepts. Figure 1. A spool and the filament’s cross-section. Tolerance describes how much the average diameter may drift; ovality describes how far from a perfect circle the wire is. Both change how much plastic leaves the nozzle. Diameter and tolerance The extruder meters plastic by length , not by volume. The slicer assumes a diameter (usually 1.75 mm) and computes how many millimeters to feed. If the real wire is 1.80 mm, the cross-sectional area is about 6% too large, and so is the amount of plastic extruded. That shows up as slightly over-extruded, bulgy surfaces. A thin spot at 1.70 mm gives the opposite: gaps and weak walls. Good filament holds ±0.02 mm; budget filament is often ±0.05 mm; anything wider is a risk. A calibrated flow ratio per material (see Calibration playbook ) absorbs the average error but not diameter swings along the spool. 1.75 mm standard diameter ±0.02–0.05 typical tolerance (mm) 1 kg common spool net weight ~330 m length of 1 kg of PLA at 1.75 mm Length per kilogram Density sets the length: PLA (1.24 g/cm³) gives roughly 330 m per kg, PETG (1.27) about 320 m, ABS (1.04) about 400 m, and carbon-fiber nylon (around 1.1–1.2) 340–370 m. Light plastics like ABS and PP go further per spool, which is why price per kg is not the same as price per part. The spool The spool is not just packaging: it is part of the system. Its core diameter determines how tightly the filament is bent. Stiff materials like PC, PA-CF and PLA-CF dislike tight cores and can snap while being unrolled. The spool’s flange, hole size and width decide whether it fits an AMS, a dryer or a side-mounted holder. Refill spools without a reel exist for the Bambu ecosystem; you reuse a reel and save plastic and money. A spool’s weight label includes only the plastic. The empty reel weighs 150–250 g, which matters when you weigh a spool to estimate what is left. Color, pigments and additives A “pure” polymer is typically translucent or milky. Color comes from pigments or dyes compounded into the plastic before extrusion. Additives change behavior as well: Property modifiers Impact modifiers (rubber particles) make “Tough PLA”; plasticizers soften; nucleating agents speed crystallization (sharper detail, less warp in some PLA); flame retardants make V-0 grades. Fillers and fibers Chopped carbon or glass fiber (stiffness, low warp, abrasive), wood flour, ground metal, stone powder, glow pigment (strontium aluminate, abrasive), magnetic or conductive particles. Process aids Lubricants and flow improvers for high-speed PLA, anti-oxidants and stabilizers against heat degradation, UV stabilizers in ASA. Visual effects Silk (shiny, usually PLA with a modifier), matte (mineral fillers), sparkle, galaxy, marble, dual-color and gradient wraps. They may print at different settings than the base polymer. Two spools of “PLA” from different brands can therefore differ more than two different polymers from the same brand. Pigment matters too: black and white are often noticeably different in flow and strength from natural or other colors, and carbon-black pigment can change heat absorption. Always treat a new brand, and even a new color, as a new material to tune (see calibration ). 🔧 Polymer science in plain language A plastic is a polymer : a very long molecular chain built from thousands of repeating units. How those chains are arranged and how they move when heated explains stiffness, heat resistance, shrinkage, clarity, chemical resistance and even how hard the material is to print. Amorphous vs semi-crystalline Chains either stay in a random tangle ( amorphous ) or partly fold into tidy, tightly packed regions called crystallites ( semi-crystalline ). Real plastics are a spectrum, but the two families behave differently when cooled. Figure 2. In amorphous plastics (PLA as printed, PETG, ABS, ASA, PC) the chains stay random. In semi-crystalline plastics (nylon, PP, PEEK, PPS, PET) part of the chain packs into ordered crystals that act like tiny reinforcing anchors. Amorphous Softens gradually over a range of temperature. Shrinks little (0.3–0.8%), warps moderately, bonds nicely between layers. Often transparent-capable. Typical: ABS, ASA, PC, PETG, PCTG, HIPS, PEI, PVA (partly). Semi-crystalline Stays stiff above its glass transition until close to the melting point, then turns thin and watery. Shrinks strongly as crystal

x: PLA, PETG & everyday plastics · 3D Printing Compendium Part 2 · Materials PLA, PETG & everyday plastics The three plastics behind most of the world’s 3D prints: how each one works, how to tune it, where it fails, and how to fix the usual problems. Beginner ⏱ 35 min read What you will learn What makes PLA, PETG and PCTG different, and which to pick for a job. The whole PLA family (plus, tough, high-speed, matte, silk, marble, wood, CF, aero, glow, color-change) and the quirks of each. Starting settings for temperature, cooling, retraction, speed and bed, and how to adjust them. How to anneal PLA, fix material-specific faults, store spools and see through common myths. 🔰 Why these three If you print for a year, roughly nine parts in ten will probably be PLA or PETG. They print at moderate temperatures on almost any machine, do not need an enclosure, and are inexpensive. PCTG, a close cousin of PETG, is increasingly popular for tougher parts. Before engineering materials make sense ( Engineering plastics ), you should be comfortable with these three. A good rule: start with PLA, move to PETG when you need heat resistance up to about 70 °C, toughness or outdoor tolerance, and only then think about anything harder . A comparison of every material is on the overview page . ~55–60 °C PLA softening (Tg) ~70–80 °C PETG / PCTG softening 190–270 °C nozzle range across the family 0.3–0.5 % typical shrinkage (low warping) 🟢 PLA: the friendly one PLA (polylactic acid) is a polyester made from fermented plant sugars (corn, sugarcane, cassava). It melts at low temperature, shrinks very little, and adheres to almost any clean bed, so it is the easiest filament to print. It is rigid and takes sharp detail, and it comes in more colors and finishes than any other material. Its two weaknesses are low heat resistance (it softens at about 55–60 °C) and brittleness: it snaps rather than bends. Figure 1. PLA is bio-based, but bio-based is not the same as biodegradable at home. It breaks down quickly only in industrial composting, which most printers do not have access to. What PLA is good at, and what it is not Strengths Easiest to print; low nozzle and bed temperature Very low warp; no enclosure required Stiff, crisp detail and sharp corners Huge range of colors and finishes Inexpensive; plant-derived Low odor while printing Limits Softens around 55–60 °C: cars, kettles, radiators, direct sun Brittle: snaps under impact or flexing Creeps under constant load, even below Tg Poor UV and outdoor lifetime (months, not years) Weak to many solvents; hydrolyzes when wet and warm Not suitable for sliding or wear The creep problem (🔧 intermediate) Plastics under steady load deform slowly. That is creep . It speeds up dramatically as the temperature nears the glass transition. A PLA clip that holds a weight happily at 20 °C may stretch noticeably at 40 °C within days and give way at 55 °C within hours. Any part that carries a continuous load (springs, hooks, belt clamps, shelves, bike mounts) needs a material with a margin: PETG for modest load, ABS/ASA, nylon or CF-composites for more. Figure 2. Creep curves for a loaded PLA bracket (schematic). The same load that is harmless at room temperature can destroy the part in hot weather. Warm environments multiply creep much faster than they reduce strength. 🧬 The PLA family “PLA” on a spool is rarely the plain polymer. Manufacturers blend in modifiers, fillers and pigments to give different looks and behaviors. Think of the base polymer as a canvas: the additive determines the quirk. Figure 3. Each PLA variant adds one idea to the same base polymer. The base’s weakness (low Tg) is shared by all, except where fillers or annealing help a little. Variant What it is Typical nozzle Behavior and quirks Best for PLA (basic) Plain PLA with pigment 200–225 °C Reference material; extremely forgiving. Everything first PLA+ PLA with a modest toughener 205–230 °C Better layer bond, less brittle; marginally hotter and stringier. “+” is not a standard: brands differ. Functional desk parts, clips Tough PLA PLA with a stronger impact modifier 210–235 °C Bends before breaking; lower stiffness; higher friction; may need a slightly slower print. Snap fits, hinges, housings High-speed PLA PLA tuned for low melt viscosity 210–240 °C Prints well at 250–500 mm/s on fast machines; needs strong cooling and a high-flow nozzle to pay off. Large, fast prints Matte PLA Mineral-filled, low sheen 200–230 °C Hides layer lines and small flaws; often slightly more brittle and stiffer; shows scratches and fingerprints. Display, enclosures Silk PLA Glossy blend, metallic look 210–235 °C Excellent shine. Runs best slower; bonds between layers worse, so weaker and more flexible; can string; poor overhang finish. Vases, figurines, decor Marble / stone PLA with fine mineral particles 205–230 °C Speckled look, sandable; mildly abrasive; avoid 0.2 mm nozzles; more brittle. Statues, planters Wood-lite PLA with 10–30 % wood fiber 190–215 °C Too hot burns the fibers (dark brown, smell); retracts poorly; a 0.4 mm nozzle can clog, so 0.6 mm is safer; varying temperature varies the shade. Decor, sign letters PLA-CF Chopped carbon fiber 210–240 °C Very stiff, matte, nearly zero warp, brittle across layers; fibers wear brass out, so use a hardened nozzle; dry it well. Stiff brackets, drone frames PLA Aero / foaming PLA with a foaming agent Hot: 230–260 °C Temperature controls expansion and density; reduce flow to compensate; about half the weight; weak surface; not good with abrasion or tight bends in feeding paths. RC planes, lightweight models Glow-in-the-dark PLA with phosphor 205–230 °C Phosphor particles (strontium aluminate) abrade brass quickly; use a hardened nozzle; charge under bright light; glow lasts minutes to hours. Signs, toys, night markers Color-change Thermochromic or photochromic pigment 200–225 °C Thermochromic parts change color with temperature (often around 25–30 °C); photochromic parts react to UV. x: Engineering plastics · 3D Printing Compendium Part 2 · Materials Engineering plastics Parts that live in hot cars, carry real loads, resist oil and sun, or replace metal: how ABS, ASA, PC, nylon, PET-CF, PPS-CF and carbon-fiber composites behave, and how a heated chamber changes the game. Intermediate ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn Why chamber temperature controls warping, layer bonding and cracking. Properties, settings and pitfalls of ABS, ASA, PC, PC-ABS, PA6/PA66/PA12/PAHT, PET-CF, PPS-CF, PP and an overview of POM, PEI and PEEK. How carbon and glass fiber change stiffness, anisotropy and nozzle wear. Adhesion aids, drying, vapor smoothing, annealing, fume safety and ready-to-use print recipes. 🔰 What makes a plastic “engineering” Everyday plastics ( PLA and PETG ) are easy but limited: they soften below 80 °C and fatigue quickly. Engineering plastics are the next tier: they stay stiff at higher temperatures, resist wear, impact, chemicals or UV, and can be used as functional parts for years. The price is difficulty. Most of them shrink more , need heat around the part , absorb water and demand hardware beyond a basic open printer: an enclosure, 260–300 °C nozzles, hardened nozzles for fiber fills, and a dryer. If you are new to materials, read the overview first, especially the sections on glass transition and crystallization , because those two ideas explain almost every rule on this page. 90–110 °C bed for ABS / ASA 260–300 °C nozzle for PC, PA, PAHT-CF up to 65 °C X2D actively heated chamber 0.5–2 % typical shrinkage range 🌡️ Chamber temperature: the big idea Hot plastic shrinks as it cools. The faster and more unevenly it cools, the more internal stress locks in. That stress shows up as warping (corners lifting), cracking between layers, and delamination (layers splitting). In a cold room the part’s surface is cooled by air at 20–25 °C while the bottom is held at 100 °C by the bed: a large gradient. In a warm chamber the air itself is 45–65 °C, the gradient shrinks, and the part cools slowly and evenly. Figure 1. The same part in two environments. Warm surrounding air does not melt the plastic (it stays below Tg) but keeps the layers from freezing before they weld to each other. Bambu X2D: an actively heated chamber The X2D’s chamber is actively heated up to 65 °C (not merely warmed by the bed), with dual-intake cooling for the opposite case when you print PLA. That makes it one of the few desktop printers able to hold PC, nylon and fiber-filled filaments at their preferred chamber temperatures. Step-by-step workflows are in Engineering materials & chamber . Chambers on bed-heated-only printers typically reach 35–55 °C after a long soak; an open-frame printer cannot reach them at all. Figure 2. Why “just open the door” fails for hard materials: the interlayer weld, and therefore the Z strength, improves substantially as the chamber warms. 🔧 Chamber heat-soak, in practice Preheat the bed to its final temperature Close all doors and lids and keep the cooling fans off. The bed does most of the early heating. Soak 15–30 minutes A large printer needs this to bring chamber air and the frame up to temperature. An actively heated chamber is faster. Heat the nozzle last Raise it to its print temperature at the end of the soak so filament does not cook inside it. Print with little or no part-cooling fan 0–30 % for ABS, ASA, PC, nylon. Use the fan briefly only for bridges and small layers. Cool down slowly When the print ends, leave the door shut until the chamber drops below roughly 40 °C. Pulling a hot big part out into room air can crack or warp it. Figure 3. Typical soak profile for a warm-chamber job (schematic). Starting before the chamber is warm is the cheapest way to get a warped first few millimeters. 🔥 ABS and ASA ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene) is the classic engineering filament: tough, machinable, sandable, heat resistant to about 95–105 °C, and soluble in acetone, which allows vapor smoothing and gluing. It also shrinks about 0.7–1 %, warps readily, and gives off a noticeable fume. ASA (acrylonitrile styrene acrylate) swaps the rubbery butadiene for an acrylic rubber and so resists UV and weather for years. It is otherwise printed just like ABS, with a little less warp and a hotter nozzle. For anything that lives outdoors (car trim, garden gear, antenna housings), choose ASA. ABS in one paragraph Nozzle 240–260 °C, bed 90–110 °C, fan 0–30 %, chamber 40–65 °C ideal. Strong, tough, cheap. Weak points: warping, odor (styrene), poor UV resistance (yellows and embrittles). Excellent when you need acetone smoothing or gluing. ASA in one paragraph Nozzle 240–270 °C, bed 90–110 °C, fan 0–30 %, chamber 40–65 °C ideal. Same as ABS plus UV and weather stability and often a more even finish. Weak points: similar fumes, brittleness when very cold, dislikes wet storage. Tips for both: use a brim of 5–10 mm, round sharp corners (r ≥ 2 mm), avoid large flat bottoms (add chamfer or “mouse ears”), keep cooling low, and avoid drafts when you open the door. For very large parts, orient so the largest flat face is not on the bed. HIPS as ABS support HIPS (high-impact polystyrene) prints at ABS temperatures and dissolves in d-limonene (a citrus solvent). It is used as a dissolvable support for ABS and ASA on a dual-nozzle or multi-material printer (see support materials ). 💎 PC and PC-ABS Polycarbonate (PC) is the toughest of the common filaments: a transparent-capable plastic used for helmets and bullet-resistant windows. Its Tg is about 140–150 °C, so printed PC stays stiff to 110–140 °C. PC prints at 260–300 °C with a bed of 100–120 °C, and it is very sensitive to moisture and drafts . It needs a warm chamber (ideally 50–65 °C or more), thorough drying, and a bed surface that grips it. Parts shrink about 0.5–0.8 %. Poor drying shows up as foam-like bubbles and fragile layers; a cold chamber causes cracks and curled corners. PC-ABS alloys blend the two. They print more easily (250–280

h: 🧽 Flexible filaments: TPU, TPE and friends
x: Flexibles & specialty filaments · 3D Printing Compendium Part 2 · Materials Flexibles & specialty filaments Rubber-like TPU, soluble supports, glowing, color-changing, wood-filled, conductive and foaming filaments: what each one really is, how to run it, and the specific quirk that will bite you. Intermediate ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn Read the Shore A / Shore D hardness scale and pick the right TPU. Print flexibles reliably: path, speed, retraction, drying and AMS limits. Use soluble, breakaway and interface supports and understand why dual-material interfaces work. Handle each specialty filament’s pitfalls, with a quick “weird filaments” cheat chart. 🧽 Flexible filaments: TPU, TPE and friends TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) and TPE (thermoplastic elastomer, a broader family that includes TPU, TPC and SEBS-based blends) are rubbery at room temperature but melt like any thermoplastic. They consist of hard, crystalline segments that act as physical crosslinks and soft, stretchy segments that give the elasticity. A higher proportion of soft segments gives a softer, more stretchy material and a harder print job. Strengths: abrasion resistance, impact and fatigue resistance, grip, vibration damping, good chemical resistance to oils and greases, hydrolysis resistance (for polyether grades). Limits: low stiffness, creep, difficult to print fast, strongly hygroscopic, low heat resistance (softens around 80–100 °C, depending on grade), sticky on some build plates. Typical uses: phone cases, gaskets, bumpers, wheels and tires for RC cars, belts, vibration feet, grips, hinges, protective covers. Shore hardness Flexible plastics are rated by Shore durometer : a spring-loaded indenter is pushed into the material and the depth is read as 0–100. Shore A covers soft to medium rubbers; Shore D covers harder plastics. The scales overlap loosely and are not exactly convertible: 95A is roughly 45D. Figure 1. Shore scale with typical examples. Datasheets sometimes quote A and D interchangeably, so check the letter. Grade Feel Print difficulty Nozzle / bed (°C) Speed (typical) Typical use TPU 98A–64D Semi-flexible, “tough plastic” Easy 220–240 / 30–60 60–120 mm/s Hinges, brackets, protective cases TPU 95A Firm rubber Easy–medium 220–240 / 30–60 30–80 mm/s Gaskets, belts, wheels TPU 90A Rubber Medium 215–235 / 30–60 20–50 mm/s Phone cases, feet TPU 85A Soft rubber Hard 210–230 / 30–60 10–35 mm/s Seals, grips, soft toys TPE 60A–80A Very soft Very hard 200–230 / 30–60 10–25 mm/s Specialty pads; often needs direct feed from an external spool 🛠️ Printing flexibles The difficulty is not melting TPU but pushing it . A soft filament behaves like a noodle: it compresses and buckles between the extruder gear and the nozzle whenever there is a gap or high resistance. The fix is a short, fully constrained filament path. Figure 2. Path length is everything. Direct drive handles even 85A TPU slowly; long Bowden systems struggle below 95A. Core settings Speed: limit volumetric flow to about 2–6 mm³/s for 85–95A TPU (a 0.4 mm nozzle with 0.2 mm layers at 0.45 mm line width is roughly 35–65 mm/s at 3–6 mm³/s). Bambu’s high-flow TPU 95A HF is the exception and will reach higher flow rates. Retraction: keep it small (0.5–1.5 mm) and slow, or disable it for very soft grades. Large, fast retractions pull the soft filament into a wad (“tangle” inside the extruder). Temperature: 210–240 °C. Hotter lowers viscosity and reduces stringing but can degrade the polymer. Cooling: 30–100 % fan works fine for TPU: it solidifies quickly and sheds heat poorly. Use more cooling for overhangs. Bed: 30–60 °C; TPU can stick extremely well to PEI. Use a release layer on smooth plates, or a textured plate without glue (see below). Infill: gyroid at 10–30 % for flexible parts gives a springy, isotropic feel; rectilinear gives directional stiffness. More walls = stiffer part. Figure 3. Soft filaments set a lower speed ceiling. Start slow and increase until you see under-extrusion or grinding. Bed adhesion, drying, and storage TPU welds to PEI. Do not add glue on textured PEI (it over-bonds and may tear the plate), but apply a thin layer of glue or a release agent on smooth PEI, engineering or high-temperature plates. Dry TPU before use (typical 50–70 °C for 4–8 h; Bambu’s own guidance for its TPU is 70 °C for 8 h in a forced-air oven, with warnings that spools expand and may deform) and store below ≈ 20 % RH in a sealed box with desiccant. TPU swells with moisture and prints foamy and stringy. Read the drying chapter . Bambu X2D and TPU On the X2D, print TPU on the main nozzle only : the right auxiliary extruder has higher feed resistance and does not support TPU. Hardness and hotend rules (for example TPU 85A needs a 0.6 mm or larger hotend; 90A can use 0.4 mm; high-flow 95A HF and “TPU for AMS” run on 0.4–0.8 mm) are in the official guide summarized in TPU & flexibles on the X2D . Only the stiffer grades labeled for the AMS belong in it; feed everything softer from the external spool. AMS and flexibles The AMS pushes and pulls filament along a PTFE tube with a defined friction budget. TPU 95A and “TPU for AMS” grades are formulated for this and have a stiffer, slicker body. Softer grades (85A–90A) can be used with the AMS only when the vendor specifically says so; otherwise they kink and jam in the buffer. Keep spools dry and keep tubing curves gentle. Details: AMS 2 Pro and Filament compatibility . x: Drying & storage · 3D Printing Compendium Part 2 · Materials Drying & storage Wet filament is the most common hidden cause of bad prints. Learn why plastics drink water from the air, how to spot it, how to dry each material safely, and how to keep it dry afterward. Beginner ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn Why polymers absorb moisture and which ones are the worst. The symptoms of wet filament and three tests to confirm it. Drying temperatures and times for each material, and the traps (spool softening, oven errors). Dryer types, storage methods and a simple moisture budget calculation. 🔬 Hygroscopy: why plastic drinks water A hygroscopic material pulls water vapor out of the air. In polymers the cause is chemistry: chains that contain polar groups (amide –CONH– in nylon, ester –COO– in PLA, PET and PETG, urethane in TPU, hydroxyl –OH in PVA and BVOH) form hydrogen bonds with water molecules and let them diffuse into the amorphous regions. Non-polar polymers such as polypropylene and polystyrene hardly absorb any. The amount depends on relative humidity (RH) , temperature and time. At equilibrium, the water content is a fixed percentage of the filament’s weight for a given RH; to reach it takes hours to weeks, depending on diameter and how tightly the spool is wound. Figure 1. Approximate equilibrium moisture content. Absolute numbers differ by grade, but the ranking is reliable: PVA and BVOH ≫ nylon ≫ TPU, PETG, PC, PLA ≫ PP. What the water does In the hotend: water flashes to steam at 200–300 °C, makes bubbles inside the molten plastic, and bursts out of the nozzle (popping, hissing, tiny craters). Hydrolysis: at high temperature, water breaks ester and amide bonds. Chains shorten, so PETG, PET, PC, PLA, PA and TPU print weaker, and the damage is permanent. This is why wet PC or PET makes brittle parts even when they look fine. Lower viscosity: hydrolyzed polymer flows too easily, which creates stringing and blobs. Post-print: parts keep absorbing moisture: nylon swells and softens; PVA turns sticky. Figure 2. Illustration of how a trace of water becomes steam inside the hotend. The part ends up with voids and visible blemishes. 🔍 Symptoms of wet filament Symptom What you see or hear Usually worst in Popping / crackling Audible snaps at the nozzle; tiny spits of plastic PETG, nylon, TPU, PVA, PC Steam White vapor at the nozzle, especially after a retraction Nylon, PVA, PC Stringing and wisps Hair-like threads between features despite good retraction PETG, TPU, PLA Rough, fuzzy or bumpy surface Craters, blisters, matte patches; dull layers All Weak or brittle parts Layers split easily; filament snaps when bent PC, PET, nylon, PLA Inconsistent extrusion Gaps, under-extrusion, blobs Nylon, TPU Bubbles in a translucent print Visible voids in clear materials PC, PETG Nozzle clog Slumping and clogs from degraded polymer PVA, BVOH, PC Many of the same defects have other causes. Pops and steam strongly indicate moisture, while pure stringing can equally be temperature or retraction. See Troubleshooting to separate them. The cheapest way to find out is to dry a sample and reprint. Figure 3. Schematic of how the surface changes as moisture rises (stylized illustration, not photographs). 🎯 Humidity targets Humidity is the storage target; it sets how fast filament re-absorbs water. Lower is always better, but the benefit depends on the material: Material Storage RH target Sensitivity Comment PVA, BVOH < 10 % Extreme Keep sealed; print from a heated dry box. Nylon (PA6, PA66, PAHT) < 15 % Very high Foams within hours in humid air. TPU / TPE < 20 % High Bambu advises < 20 % RH in a sealed box with desiccant. PC, PC-ABS, PET-CF < 20 % High Hydrolysis ruins strength. PETG, PCTG < 25 % Medium-high Pops and strings quickly. ABS, ASA < 30 % Medium Surface rough when wet. PLA < 30–40 % Low-medium Tolerant for weeks; but wet PLA gets brittle and stringy. PP no strict target Low Keep clean and dust-free. Figure 4. Humidity zones by material class. A humidity reading belongs to the air inside the box ; it says little about how wet the filament already is. 🌡️ Drying temperature and time Heat increases the vapor pressure of the absorbed water and speeds its escape. The limit is the filament’s softening point: above it the spool deforms, filaments fuse together, and the loops cross-weld. Stay at least 10–15 °C below the glass transition (Tg) of the polymer, or follow the maker’s spool label. Times assume a standard 1 kg spool, ventilated dryer and mild moisture; very wet nylon or PVA can take twice as long. Material Temp (°C) Time (h) Spool caveat Tg of base (°C, approx.) PLA / PLA+ 45–55 4–8 Tg ≈ 60 °C; above 55 °C the spool may soften and warp. ≈ 60 Silk / wood / filled PLA 40–50 4–8 Stay cooler; wood fillers can darken. ≈ 55–60 PETG / PCTG 60–65 4–8 Tg ≈ 80 °C, so 65 °C is safe. ≈ 80 TPU / TPE 50–65 (some vendors up to 70) 6–10 Softens; spools can swell by a few mm. Check the vendor. (rubbery) ABS / ASA 70–80 4–6 Cardboard or thin spools may deform. ≈ 105 PC / PC-ABS 80 8 Needs a dryer that holds temperature. Bambu gives 80 °C, 8 h for its PC. ≈ 145 / ≈ 110 PA6 / PA66 / PAHT 80–90 8–12 Fastest drying is above 80 °C; only on heat-resistant spools. ≈ 50–70 (dry) PA12 70–80 6–8 Moderate. ≈ 45–50 PET-CF / PET 65–80 6–10 Also dry before crystallization is complete; fine. ≈ 80 PPS-CF 100–140 8–12 Bambu’s figure; only on spools rated for it (Bambu: never above 160 °C). ≈ 90 PP 50–60 3–4 Rarely needed. ≈ −10 PVA 45–55 6–12 Gets sticky; do not exceed 55 °C. ≈ 75 BVOH 45–60 6–12 Follow maker. ≈ 60–70 HIPS 60–65 4–6 Low sensitivity. ≈ 100 Why drying temperature has a ceiling Heating PLA to 70 °C on a spool is a classic mistake: the polymer is above its Tg, the spool relaxes, loops fuse and the filament can no longer unwind. x: Slicers compared · 3D Printing Compendium Part 3 · Software Slicers compared A slicer turns a 3D model into the thousands of tiny movements your printer actually performs. Learn what it does, how the popular ones differ, how to read their interface, and how to work in a way that avoids failed prints. Beginner Intermediate ⏱ 35 min read What you will learn What happens between "File → Open" and a finished print, and why a slicer is needed at all. How Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer, PrusaSlicer, Cura, SuperSlicer, Simplify3D and online slicers differ. How to find your way around any modern slicer: object list, plate, preview, presets. How profiles and project files ( .3mf , .gcode.3mf ) work and how to share them safely. A repeatable slicing workflow, plus what is special about the Bambu Lab X2D. What a slicer does 🔰 The plain-language version Your printer cannot understand a 3D model directly. A model (usually an STL or 3MF file) is only a description of a surface : a skin made of thousands of small triangles. A printer, on the other hand, needs a long list of simple instructions such as "move to X=100, Y=80 while pushing out 0.4 mm of plastic". The program that converts one into the other is called a slicer , because its core trick is to cut the model into thin horizontal layers, much like slicing a loaf of bread, and then work out how to draw each slice with a thin line of molten plastic. The output of a slicer is G-code (see G-code, firmware & ecosystem ), a text-like list of commands that the printer firmware executes line by line. Everything you set in the slicer (layer height, wall count, infill, speeds, temperatures, supports) ends up as numbers inside this file. Figure 1. The slicing pipeline. A triangle mesh is cut into thin layers, each layer is filled with extrusion paths, and the paths are converted into machine commands. 🔧 What the slicer actually computes Behind the friendly buttons a slicer solves several distinct problems, and knowing them helps you understand why a setting exists: Intersect the mesh with planes. For each layer height step the slicer finds where the triangles cross the plane. The result is a set of closed 2D outlines (polygons). Holes become inner outlines. This is why a mesh must be watertight : an open edge means the outline cannot close (see File formats & mesh repair ). Classify regions. Each polygon is analyzed against the layers above and below. Areas with nothing below are overhangs (they need support or bridging), areas with air above are top surfaces , and the rest is interior . Generate perimeters (walls). The outline is offset inward by one line width at a time to create the outer wall and inner walls. Modern slicers use variable width algorithms (Arachne) to fill thin features cleanly. Fill the interior. The remaining area gets sparse infill in a chosen pattern, plus solid infill for the top and bottom shells. Plan supports, brims and skirts. Support columns, interface layers, and adhesion aids are generated per layer. Order and optimize the paths. The slicer decides where each loop starts (the seam ), which line to print first, when to retract, when to lift the nozzle and how to avoid crossing walls. Assign speeds, temperatures and cooling. Each feature type gets its speed and acceleration, layers that finish too fast are slowed, and fan speeds are set. Emit G-code. Finally, every path is converted to G1 moves with an extrusion amount calculated from line width, layer height and filament diameter. How much plastic is "E"? The slicer calculates the extrusion for each move from the volume of the line. A 0.42 mm wide, 0.2 mm tall line that is 10 mm long has a volume of about 0.42 × 0.2 × 10 ≈ 0.84 mm³ (a rounded-rectangle model gives slightly less). A 1.75 mm filament has a cross-section of about 2.405 mm², so the feed length is about 0.35 mm. Multiply by your flow ratio and you have the E value in the G-code. The slicer landscape There are dozens of slicers, but almost all of them descend from a few families. Knowing the lineage tells you which interface and feature set to expect. Figure 2. Simplified slicer family tree. Slic3r-lineage slicers share a similar layout, terminology and many setting names, so skills transfer easily between them. Meet the slicers Bambu Studio Free, open source (AGPL), by Bambu Lab. Best integration with Bambu printers: cloud/LAN sending, AMS color mapping, MakerWorld, filament RFID profiles, and the X2D's dual-nozzle logic. Based on PrusaSlicer's code base. OrcaSlicer Free, open source fork of Bambu Studio with support for many brands (Bambu, Prusa, Creality, Voron/Klipper, Anycubic…). Famous for its built-in calibration wizards (flow, pressure advance, temperature, retraction, max volumetric speed) and extra tuning options. PrusaSlicer Free, open source, by Prusa Research. Mature and polished, excellent documentation, strong profiles for Prusa printers, variable layer height, modifiers, multi-material and Arachne wall generator. Also runs other Marlin and Klipper printers. UltiMaker Cura Free, open source, huge community and by far the largest list of ready-made machine profiles. Simple "recommended" mode, deep "custom" mode with thousands of settings, and a plug-in marketplace (post-processing scripts, Arachne origin). SuperSlicer Community fork of PrusaSlicer with extra expert options: built-in calibration prints, more infill patterns, more seam and thin-wall tweaks. Development is slower than the main projects, so check activity before committing to it. Simplify3D Commercial, paid slicer from the early 2010s era, once the go-to "pro" tool with powerful manual support placement and process-per-layer-range. Updates have been sparse; today most users have moved to free alternatives. Treat as legacy. Kiri:Moto & online slicers Browser-based slicers (Kiri:Moto is the best known) need no installation, run on Chromebooks and tablets, and are handy for a quick job. x: Slicer settings explained · 3D Printing Compendium Part 3 · Software Slicer settings explained Hundreds of sliders, dozens that matter, a handful that decide most of your results. This page explains each important setting in plain language, with typical values, the trade-offs, and pictures of what actually changes inside the print. Beginner Intermediate Advanced ⏱ 55 min read How to use this page Skim the priority pyramid first. It tells you where to spend your attention. Each setting lives in a collapsible panel with the same four rows: What it does , Typical , Change it when , Trade-offs . Names vary slightly between Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer, PrusaSlicer and Cura; the descriptions use the most common wording. Values are starting points for a 0.4 mm nozzle on a well-tuned printer. Tune from there, one change at a time, and check the starting profiles at the bottom. Where to focus: the priority pyramid A slicer exposes an overwhelming number of settings, but they do not all matter equally. A wrong filament temperature ruins a print; a slightly different seam gap does not. Work from the base of the pyramid upward: only fine-tune the tip after everything beneath it is right. Figure 1. Settings that matter most sit at the bottom. If your first layer or filament profile is wrong, no amount of seam tuning or ironing will rescue the print. 🔰 Vocabulary you will see everywhere Perimeter / wall / loop A closed line of plastic following the outline of a layer. "Wall loops" and "perimeters" mean the same thing. Infill The pattern that fills the inside of the part, mostly air with thin lines of plastic to hold the walls up. Shell The solid skin: walls plus the top and bottom solid layers. Together they carry most of the strength. Line width How wide each extruded line is, normally 100–125 % of the nozzle diameter. Extrusion multiplier / flow ratio A scale factor on the amount of plastic extruded; 1.0 = theoretical amount, tuned per filament. Volumetric speed Plastic volume per second (mm³/s); the true limit of a hotend, more meaningful than mm/s. Anatomy of a printed part Before the individual settings, picture what a slice looks like from the side. Every setting below acts on some part of this cross-section. Figure 2. The anatomy of a slice. Red: outer wall. Purple: inner walls. Teal: sparse infill. Orange: solid top and bottom layers. Yellow: brim lines on the first layer. Quality settings These control the resolution and finish of the surface: how smooth, how accurate and how clean it looks. Layer height 🔰 Layer height 0.08–0.32 mm (0.4 mm nozzle: 0.20 mm) What it does Sets the thickness of each layer (the Z distance between slice planes). Thinner layers make smaller steps on curved and sloped surfaces; thicker layers print faster. Typical 0.12 mm fine, 0.16 mm quality, 0.20 mm standard , 0.24 mm functional, 0.28–0.32 mm draft. A good range is 25–75 % of the nozzle diameter; 0.4 mm nozzles work from roughly 0.08 to 0.30 mm. Change it when Fine details, small text, curved figures or smooth threads call for 0.08–0.16 mm. Large functional parts that will be sanded or hidden suit 0.24–0.32 mm. Tall thin prints can benefit from thicker layers to reduce vibration time. Trade-offs Print time scales roughly with 1/layer height: halving it about doubles print time. Thick layers have stronger inter-layer bonds per line (more contact area per line) but visible banding; very thin layers on a 0.4 nozzle may have flow problems. Figure 3. Stair-stepping on a 45° surface (steps drawn at 100× scale). Notice how the error shrinks with layer height; near-vertical and near-horizontal surfaces show almost no stair-stepping, shallow slopes show the most. Adaptive / variable layer height Rather than one layer height for the whole part, let the slicer use thin layers on curved or shallow areas and thick layers on vertical walls. In Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer it is under the "adaptive layer height" or "variable layer height" tool; in Cura it is "Use adaptive layers". Expect 10–40 % time saving compared with using the fine height everywhere. First-layer height, width and speed 🔰 Initial layer height 0.20–0.30 mm What it does Sets the thickness of the very first layer. A slightly thicker first layer is more forgiving of a bed that is a little uneven, and sticks better because the line is squeezed wide. Typical 0.20 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle (0.25–0.30 mm if your bed is not perfectly flat or you print big parts). Some slicers also set a wider first-layer line (e.g. 120–150 % of nozzle). Change it when Poor adhesion on large parts, slightly uneven plates, or textured plates that need more squish. Thinner (0.12–0.16 mm) for very smooth, precise bottoms on a perfectly calibrated bed. Trade-offs Thicker first layer = more tolerance but a rougher bottom and a larger elephant's foot. First-layer speed should be slow (20–50 mm/s) for good contact. The first layer is everything. See First layer & bed adhesion for squish, cleaning, glue and calibration. Line width 🔧 Line width (per feature) 100–125 % of the nozzle What it does Controls how wide each extruded line is. The slicer flattens the round filament into a rounded rectangle, so line width and layer height together decide how much plastic is laid down per mm. Typical Outer wall 0.40–0.42 mm (about 100–105 %) for crisp edges; inner wall, infill and top surface 0.42–0.50 mm; first layer 0.42–0.50 mm. For a 0.4 mm nozzle the usable range is roughly 0.35–0.60 mm. Change it when Wider lines fill thin gaps and make faster, stronger infill; narrower outer lines resolve fine detail. Using 0.6 mm lines from a 0.4 mm nozzle is a classic speed hack, but only if the hotend can melt enough plastic. Trade-offs Wider = more flow needed, faster fill, stronger bond to neighbors, softer corners. Narrower = more detail, more lines (slower), and a risk of gaps if narrower than the nozzle opening. Learn how the main families of modeling tools think, which one fits which job, and how to design a simple part that prints well on the first try. Beginner Intermediate ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn The four modeling paradigms (mesh, parametric solid, code, generative) and when each is the right tool. A fair tour of the popular programs, with strengths, limits, cost and licensing. The core CAD vocabulary: sketches, constraints, extrude, revolve, loft, sweep, fillets, booleans, patterns and assemblies. How to model for printing, measure real objects, remix safely and judge AI-generated models honestly. A complete ten-step bracket workflow, plus short OpenSCAD and CadQuery examples. Four ways to describe a shape All modeling programs end up producing a mesh that your slicer can read, but they get there by very different routes. Choosing the right route for the job saves more time than learning any particular program. Figure 1. Four paradigms. Many projects mix them: a sculpted shape for the look, a parametric model for the mechanism, code for repeating patterns. 🔰 Think "clay" or think "blueprint"? If you ask "how should it look ?" (a figurine, a creature, a smooth grip), mesh sculpting is natural. If you ask "how big must it be to fit ?" (a bracket, a case, a gear), you need exact numbers and an editable history, which is what parametric CAD or code provide. 🔧 Exact vs approximate Parametric and code models are mathematically defined (planes, cylinders, splines), and only converted to triangles when you export. Sculpted models are triangles from the start, so you cannot reliably say "make this hole 5.2 mm" without rebuilding it. Software tour No program is "the best"; each is a trade-off between ease, precision and cost. Prices and license terms change often, so treat the notes below as a snapshot to verify on the vendor's site before you commit.
