x: File formats & mesh repair · 3D Printing Compendium Part 3 · Software File formats & mesh repair Every 3D print starts with a file, and many failed prints start with a bad one. Learn which formats to use, what a healthy mesh looks like, how to find and fix problems, and how to find, license and archive models responsibly. Intermediate Advanced ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn How STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP, AMF, PLY, glTF, SVG/DXF and G-code differ, and which one to use when. What a mesh is made of, and what "manifold", "watertight" and "inverted normals" mean in practice. How to repair, simplify, hollow and split models with free tools, and what Boolean operations can break. How to read repository licenses carefully, check printability, and archive models with Git LFS and sensible names. File formats compared Formats fall into four families. Mesh formats (STL, OBJ, PLY, AMF, 3MF) store triangles. Solid (B-rep) formats (STEP, IGES, Parasolid) store exact surfaces, ideal for editing in CAD. Scene formats (glTF, OBJ with materials) store meshes plus textures for display. Instruction formats (G-code and its variants) store printer commands and are the output of the slicer, not the input. See Slicers compared for how a mesh becomes G-code. Figure 1. Where each format sits in the pipeline. Keep the exact version (STEP or native CAD) as the master and export meshes only for slicing. Format Stores Units Color / multi-material Best for Watch out for STL (.stl) Triangles only (binary or ASCII) None; assumed mm No Universal single-material exchange No units, no metadata, large files for fine curves OBJ (.obj + .mtl) Triangles/polygons, normals, UVs, material names None Via textures or material groups Sculpts, textured and colored models Polygons can be quads or n-gons; separate .mtl and texture files 3MF (.3mf) Mesh, units, build plate, colors, materials, thumbnails, slicer settings Yes (default mm) Yes Modern default for slicers; sharing projects Slicer-specific extensions; settings may not transfer between brands AMF (.amf) XML mesh with curved patches, colors, materials Yes Yes Legacy; largely superseded by 3MF Poor software support today STEP (.step/.stp) Exact B-rep geometry, assemblies Yes Limited CAD exchange and archiving Not directly printable in all slicers; tessellation settings matter IGES (.igs) Older surface/curve exchange Yes No Legacy CAD exchange Often surfaces without a closed solid Parasolid (.x_t/.x_b) Exact B-rep kernel format Yes No SolidWorks, NX, Shapr3D exchange Proprietary kernel; fewer free tools PLY (.ply) Points/triangles with vertex colors None Per-vertex color 3D scans and photogrammetry Usually needs conversion and cleanup glTF/GLB Meshes, materials, textures, animation Meters by convention Textures Web, AR and game assets Meters, not mm; can be non-manifold and non-solid SVG / DXF 2D vector paths Yes (DXF), varies (SVG) No Logos, laser cutters, extrusions Needs closed, clean paths and correct scaling G-code (.gcode) Printer commands mm Via tool changes Direct printing Printer-specific; not a model The three-file habit For each project keep: (1) the native CAD or script file, (2) a STEP export for portability, and (3) the 3MF project you actually sliced. STL is an acceptable throw-away export, not an archive. G-code flavors and containers Plain .gcode files are text and can be read in any editor. .bgcode is a compact binary G-code format designed to cut file size and speed uploads on printers that support it (introduced by Prusa for its firmware). Bambu Lab printers use .gcode.3mf : a 3MF package containing the plate's G-code, thumbnails and metadata, which is what Bambu Studio sends to the printer. These containers are described in G-code, firmware & ecosystem . Never edit a file you do not understand and never run G-code from an untrusted source on a printer you care about. Mesh anatomy A mesh is a surface described by three things: vertices (points in space), edges (lines between two vertices) and faces (usually triangles bounded by three edges). Each face has an outward-pointing normal , a direction perpendicular to the face that tells the software which side is "outside". A printable mesh must enclose a volume unambiguously. Figure 2. The building blocks of a mesh. Outward normals tell the slicer which side of a face is solid material. Manifold and watertight, explained A mesh is manifold when every edge is shared by exactly two faces, and the faces around each vertex form a single connected fan. It is watertight when it has no holes, so water poured inside could not leak. Slicers compute the interior by counting how many surfaces a ray crosses; if the surface has holes, overlaps or flipped faces, the count goes wrong, and the slicer may print nothing, fill the wrong region or produce odd gaps. Figure 3. Six problems that confuse slicers. Most can be fixed automatically; non-manifold edges and self-intersections often need manual attention. Symptom in the slicer Likely mesh cause First thing to try "Object has errors" or auto-repair warning Holes, non-manifold edges, inverted normals Accept the slicer's repair, then check the preview Part missing in preview or layers empty Flipped normals or open shell Recalculate outside normals; close holes Random gaps or lines inside walls Self-intersections or overlapping shells Boolean union in a mesh tool or CAD; remove duplicates Thin walls vanish Walls under line width Thicken in CAD or enable thin-wall detection Specks and blobs outside the part Tiny stray shells Delete tiny components in a mesh editor Huge slicing time or stutter Millions of triangles Decimate (see below) Resolution, tessellation and faceted curves A mesh made of flat triangles can only approximate a curve. x: G-code, firmware & ecosystem · 3D Printing Compendium Part 3 · Software G-code, firmware & ecosystem Behind every print is a text file of simple commands and a firmware that turns them into motor pulses and heater power. Learn to read G-code, understand how the main firmware families differ, and connect your printer to your network safely. Advanced Intermediate ⏱ 45 min read What you will learn How to read G-code, with the essential commands explained line by line, including a first-layer example. What firmware does, and how Marlin, Klipper, RepRapFirmware, Prusa, Bambu and Creality differ. Key control concepts: motion planning, pressure advance, input shaping and bed mesh compensation. Host software, network modes, security and privacy basics, monitoring and automation. How to edit start and end G-code, post-process files and debug a print by reading its G-code, safely. G-code primer G-code is a line-based language of machine commands. Each line holds a command (like G1 ) followed by parameters (letters with numbers, like X50 Y20 E0.8 F1800 ). Anything after a semicolon is a comment that the printer ignores. Your slicer writes the file; the printer's firmware reads it one line at a time and executes it. Because the language dates back to CNC machines of the 1950s, dialects differ between firmware, but the basics are shared. Figure 1. A G-code line becomes motion: parse, plan, convert to step pulses, move. Extrusion (E) is synchronized to travel so line width stays constant. Essential commands Command Meaning Example and notes G0 / G1 Move; G1 usually carries extrusion, G0 is a "rapid" move G1 X100 Y50 E2.5 F1800 . Feed rate F is in mm/min (1800 = 30 mm/s). Many firmwares treat G0 and G1 the same. G2 / G3 Arc clockwise / counter-clockwise G2 X20 Y0 I10 J0 : I, J are offsets from the start point to the arc center. Reduces file size when arc fitting is enabled. G28 Home axes G28 (all) or G28 X Y . Always the first motion of a job. G29 Bed leveling / mesh probing Marlin and some vendors use it; Klipper uses BED_MESH_CALIBRATE . Bambu start G-code also triggers leveling through its own routine. G90 / G91 Absolute / relative positioning (XYZ) Absolute is the norm; relative is used for small hops and retractions. M82 / M83 Absolute / relative extruder mode Relative ( M83 ) is preferred since E never grows large. G92 Set current position without moving G92 E0 resets the extruder counter (needed with absolute E). M104 / M109 Set hotend temperature / set and wait M104 S210 starts heating; M109 S210 blocks until reached. M140 / M190 Set bed temperature / set and wait M140 S60 then M190 S60 later. M106 / M107 Part-cooling fan speed / off M106 S255 is 100 %; S range 0–255. M106 P1 S128 can address a second fan. M204 Set acceleration M204 S3000 (some firmware uses P/T for print and travel). M205 Set jerk or junction deviation limits M205 X8 Y8 in Marlin; Klipper uses SET_VELOCITY_LIMIT instead. M900 K… Linear/pressure advance factor (Marlin, Bambu) M900 K0.04 . Klipper: SET_PRESSURE_ADVANCE ADVANCE=0.04 . RepRapFirmware: M572 D0 S0.04 . M220 / M221 Speed / flow override (percent) M221 S95 reduces flow to 95 %. M600 Filament change (pause, unload, wait) Used for color changes on single-extruder machines. T0 , T1 … Select tool/extruder Tool changers and multi-extruder machines. Dual-nozzle and AMS printers wrap tool or filament change in vendor-specific sequences (for example, Bambu uses M620 / M621 blocks, which you should not edit). G4 Dwell (wait) G4 P500 waits 500 ms. M84 Disable stepper motors End-of-print command. M73 Progress and time remaining Updates the printer display. Dialects differ A command with the same name can behave differently between firmwares, or may not exist. Always check the documentation of your printer's firmware before copying lines from forums. Arcs and relative moves Figure 2. Arc commands trade a bit of firmware complexity for smaller files and smoother motion. Check that your firmware supports arcs before enabling arc fitting. Line-by-line: a first-layer sample This simplified sample shows what a typical job looks like from the start. It is a generic, Marlin-style example for teaching, not a profile for any specific printer: real start G-code from vendors includes many extra steps. Figure 3. Anatomy of a job. Every printer's start sequence follows this skeleton, with extra vendor-specific calibration inserted. Reading E values E is the length of filament pushed, in millimeters of 1.75 mm filament. A rough check: line volume ≈ line width × layer height × length, e.g. 0.42 × 0.2 × 20 mm = 1.68 mm³. Filament cross-section for 1.75 mm is 2.405 mm², so E ≈ 1.68 ÷ 2.405 ≈ 0.70 mm; the sample's 0.66 is in the right range, with differences caused by flow ratio and line-shape assumptions. Bambu .gcode.3mf and binary G-code Bambu Studio does not send a plain text file. It produces a .gcode.3mf , which is a ZIP-compressed 3MF package containing the sliced G-code ( Metadata/plate_1.gcode and related files), plate thumbnails, per-plate settings and a checksum used by the printer. You can rename the file to .zip and open it to look at the contents. The G-code inside contains many Bambu-specific commands for calibration, AMS handling, noise and chamber control, so it will not run unchanged on other printers. Prusa printers use a different compact container: .bgcode , a binary G-code format that stores metadata and compressed blocks, and can be converted back to text with Prusa's tools. In both cases the slicer's preview, not the raw file, is the right place to inspect a job. Closed printers: look, don't edit On printers with proprietary firmware (such as Bambu Lab), the start and end sequences, AMS or tool-change blocks, calibration routines and some M commands are tightly coupled to the firmware. x: First layer & bed adhesion · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques First layer & bed adhesion Most failed prints die in the first five minutes. Learn what a perfect first layer looks like, why plastic shrinks and lifts, and how to make any material stay put and still come off cleanly. Beginner → Intermediate ⏱ 35 min read What you will learn How to read a first layer at a glance, set Z-offset by sight, choose and clean a build surface, pick the right adhesion aid for each material, use brims, rafts and mouse ears, stop elephant foot and warping, level the bed, and diagnose every common first-layer failure from a picture. Why the first layer matters so much A 3D print is a stack of thin plastic lines. Every line is glued to the one below it by heat. The very first line has nothing below it except the build plate, so it has to stick to a different material, at a different temperature, while the rest of the part tries to pull it loose. Three jobs fall on that one layer: Hold the part down against nozzle drag, travel moves and, most importantly, the internal stress created when hot plastic cools and shrinks. Provide a flat reference : every following layer copies the first one. A first layer that is 0.1 mm thicker on one side makes a tilted part, and small errors in the base get magnified into visible lean at the top. Create the visible bottom surface of your part. Whatever the bed looks like, the underside of the print looks like it too. The good news: the first layer is easy to judge by eye, and a few minutes of tuning per printer and per plate pay back on every print you make afterwards. 🔰 Vocabulary you will meet Term Meaning Z-offset A correction added to the "zero" height so that the nozzle sits the right distance above the plate for the first layer. Smaller gap = more squish. Squish How much the nozzle presses the extruded line flat against the plate. Good squish gives wide, flat, glossy-looking lines that fuse side by side. Bed / build plate / build surface The heated platform (bed) and the removable sheet (plate) on which the part is printed. Often "bed" is used for both. Brim / skirt / raft Extra perimeter lines, an outline that does not touch the part, or a thick printed base. See brims, skirts, rafts . Warping Corners or edges of the part curling upward off the bed as it cools and shrinks. Elephant foot A bulge at the bottom of a part where the first layers are squashed wider than the rest. Bed mesh A grid of height measurements the printer takes so it can follow tiny dips and bumps of the plate. Z-offset and squish: the core idea A typical first layer is set to a height of about 0.2 mm even when the rest of the print uses 0.12 mm or 0.16 mm layers, and the line is deliberately extruded a little wider than the nozzle (for example 0.5 mm wide from a 0.4 mm nozzle). The plastic leaves the nozzle as a round "noodle" and gets pressed flat by the nozzle tip as it moves. The gap between the tip and the plate determines the final shape. Figure 1. Side view of the first layer as the nozzle moves left to right. Too high and the plastic is simply laid on the plate; ideal squish presses each line into a flat ribbon; too low and plastic has nowhere to go, so it squeezes sideways and upward. How to set Z-offset by eye Print a thin test pattern Use a single-layer full-bed or large-square pattern (many slicers and printers include one; you can also print a 150 × 150 mm square, one layer thick). Clean the plate first. Watch the first lines being laid Lines should look slightly flattened and touch their neighbors. If they look like round tubes with visible gaps, lower the nozzle (more negative offset or "closer"). Adjust live in small steps Move 0.02 mm at a time. Wait one or two lines for the change to show. Larger jumps overshoot and gouge the plate. Inspect the finished sheet Hold it at an angle under light. It should be a uniform, slightly glossy skin without grooves. Run a fingernail across it: you should feel almost no ridges. Try the paper test only as a rough start On printers without auto Z, a sheet of paper that drags slightly is a starting point. Always refine by looking at real extrusion. Save it Store the value per plate (smooth PEI and textured PEI need different offsets) and note it in your calibration log . Why squish works Imagine squeezing toothpaste onto a table while dragging the tube. With the tube lifted high the paste is a fat worm that barely touches. Pressing the tip close forces the worm to spread wide and flat, increasing the contact area between plastic and plate, and pushing each line into its neighbor so they weld together. The pressure also drives molten plastic into the micro-texture of the surface, which is a big part of why adhesion improves. Common mistake Trying to cure poor adhesion with temperature or glue when the real problem is Z-offset that is 0.05–0.1 mm too high. If lines look round, fix squish first, then everything else. Squish, line width and flow: a small bit of math The slicer calculates how much plastic to extrude from the cross-section of a line. A common model treats the line as a rectangle with rounded ends: the area is roughly (width − height) × height + π × (height / 2)². For a 0.5 mm wide, 0.2 mm high line this is about 0.30 × 0.2 + 0.031 = 0.091 mm² . At 50 mm/s that is 4.6 mm³/s, easy for any hotend. If the real gap is smaller than the slicer assumes, the plastic still has to go somewhere, which is why too-low Z creates ridges and may even stop extrusion (the nozzle tip is blocked by the plate and the extruder clicks or skips). Setting Typical start Why First-layer height 0.2–0.25 mm (0.5 × nozzle diameter ≈ 0.2 for 0.4 mm) A thicker first layer tolerates small bed irregularities and has more plastic mass to grip with. x: Supports, bridges & overhangs · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques Supports, bridges & overhangs A printer cannot print in thin air. Learn exactly how far plastic can reach beyond the layer below, how to bridge gaps, when to add supports, which kind to choose, and how to design parts so you hardly need them. Beginner → Intermediate ⏱ 35 min read What you will learn The geometry behind the 45° rule, how bridging really works and how to tune it, the support styles in modern slicers (normal, tree, snug, interface layers, soluble), Z-gap and interface settings, removal tools, paint-on supports, design tricks that eliminate supports, and how much supports cost in time and material. Why supports exist FDM printing builds objects one layer at a time. Each new line of molten plastic needs something underneath it to land on. When there is solid material or cooled plastic below, everything works. When there is empty space below, the soft plastic droops, strings or falls. Three situations create empty space: Overhangs: surfaces that lean outward as you go up. A small lean is fine; a large lean is not. Bridges: horizontal spans between two supported points, such as the top of a doorway. Islands: parts of a layer with nothing at all below, such as the top of a floating bar. These always need support. Supports are temporary scaffolds printed underneath these features and removed afterwards. They cost time, plastic and surface quality, so the best strategy is the layered one: first design and orient to avoid them, then tune the printer so it handles small overhangs and bridges without them, and only then add supports where needed. Overhang physics 🔰 Angle versus layer offset Imagine a wall that leans outward. Each layer sits a little farther out than the one below. The amount of shift per layer depends on the lean angle and the layer height. Overhang angle in slicers is usually measured from vertical : 0° is a straight wall, 45° leans halfway, and 90° is a flat horizontal ceiling. The horizontal shift per layer is offset = layer height × tan(θ) . For 0.2 mm layers: at 30° the shift is 0.12 mm, at 45° it is 0.20 mm, at 60° it is 0.35 mm, and at 70° it is 0.55 mm. A line is about 0.4–0.45 mm wide, so the part of each new line that is actually supported by the layer below is (width − offset) / width . Once the offset exceeds the line width, nothing supports the new line from below at all. Figure 1. As the lean angle grows, each new line overlaps less with the layer below. Beyond about 60° the new line is mostly hanging in air and relies on the plastic freezing quickly before it can sag. Why it sags Fresh extrudate is a soft viscous strand at 200+ °C. Gravity pulls it down while the cooling fan and surrounding air freeze it. If the strand reaches the temperature where it stops flowing before it has sagged far, the overhang survives. That is why strong part cooling, slower speed and a cooler nozzle improve overhangs, and why thin layers (small offset per layer) overhang better than thick ones for the same angle. The 45° rule and beyond The old rule says "anything up to 45° prints without support". It is a reasonable rule of thumb for a lightly tuned printer, but there is no sharp cut-off. Surface quality gets progressively worse as angle increases. Figure 2. A practical overhang scale. With a well-tuned printer, "Tunable" angles up to about 55–60° can be clean; flat ceilings are bridges, a different problem. Angle from vertical What happens What to do 0–30° Almost indistinguishable from a vertical wall Nothing 30–45° Slightly rougher underside; visible stair-stepping Standard settings are fine; thinner layers look nicer 45–60° Droop, curling edges, fuzzy underside Max part-fan, slower overhang walls, test with an overhang ladder 60–80° Strands hang; surface looks like noodles Supports, or redesign as chamfer/bridge 80–90° (flat ceiling) Bridge behavior Bridge tuning (below) or supports 🔧 Making overhangs better without supports Cool hard. For PLA use 100 % fan after the first layers. For PETG and ABS you must balance layer adhesion and sag: use 40–70 % fan only on overhang and bridge regions if your slicer allows. Slow down for overhang walls. Many slicers can detect steep perimeters and cut speed to 10–40 mm/s there, and Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer expose this as "slow down for overhang". Use thinner layers. The horizontal offset per layer is proportional to height, so 0.12 mm layers hold a steeper angle than 0.28 mm layers. Reduce nozzle temperature by 5–10 °C for the overhang test. A cooler strand freezes sooner. Print the outer wall last? Wall order matters: printing inner walls first lets the outer wall lean on a cooled backing. "Inner/outer/inner" or "inner then outer" is a common choice for overhang quality. Reduce flow slightly on overhangs. Less plastic means less to sag. Some slicers have an overhang flow ratio. Add an extra air-cooling duct. Printers with strong dual fans or a dedicated auxiliary fan have a big advantage; see speed, cooling & quality . Bridging A bridge is a line of plastic that spans empty space between two supported points. Instead of being laid on something, it is stretched through the air like a rope. Good bridging relies on three ideas: keep the strand under tension , cool it instantly and give it solid anchors on both ends. Figure 3. A good bridge is a row of taut strands pulled straight between anchors. The slicer picks the direction that gives the shortest span and puts a separate bridge layer on top before the normal infill resumes. How bridging is set up in the slicer Detect The slicer finds areas of a layer that have no material directly below ("bridge" regions) and flags them. Choose direction Lines are aligned along the shortest path between anchors. You can often set a bridge angle manually. Print one or two bridge layers The first layer spans the gap with widely spaced, slightly thick lines at lower flow; the second bridges across the first at 90° to close

x: Speed, cooling & quality · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques Speed, cooling & quality Print faster without ruining the part. Understand what really limits speed (flow, acceleration, vibration, cooling), how to tune each limit, and how to diagnose the surface when something goes wrong. Intermediate ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn The speed–quality–strength trade-off, the volumetric flow equation and typical limits, acceleration and jerk, ringing and input shaping, pressure advance, how to cool each material, temperature towers, high-speed habits, noise, layer-height presets, adaptive layers, belt and vibration care, VFA and Z-banding, and a table of sensible speeds for each feature. 🔰 The speed – quality – strength triangle Every 3D printing profile is a compromise between three goals. You can push hard on two of them, but the third pays the price. Figure 1. Pick the corner that matters for the job and balance the other two. A decorative figurine lives near Quality; a load-bearing bracket near Strength; a quick fit test near Speed. Fast printers have shifted the whole triangle outward: a modern machine does in an hour what an older machine did in four. But the physics is unchanged, and understanding which limit you are hitting is the skill that separates tuned printers from lucky ones. There are four independent limits: Melting limit (volumetric flow) The hotend can only melt a certain volume of plastic per second. Motion limit (acceleration & vibration) The frame and belts ring when the toolhead changes direction; fast corners smear. Pressure limit (extrusion dynamics) The filament in the nozzle is compressible; flow lags commands, which bulges corners. Cooling limit The plastic must solidify before the next layer lands on it, especially for small details and overhangs. Volumetric flow: the hidden speed limit 🔰 What is volumetric flow? Speed in mm/s sounds like the natural speed measure, but the hotend does not care how fast the nozzle moves ; it cares how much plastic it must melt per second. A thin, narrow line at 300 mm/s may need less melting than a thick, wide line at 100 mm/s. That quantity is the volumetric flow rate , measured in mm³/s: The key formula Flow (mm³/s) = line width × layer height × speed. Example: 0.42 mm × 0.20 mm × 150 mm/s = 12.6 mm³/s. To find the fastest speed a hotend allows, rearrange: speed = max flow ÷ (width × height) . Figure 2. The hotend melts a volume per second. Wider or thicker lines raise the flow at the same speed, so thick layers hit the flow limit at much lower travel speeds than thin layers. Maximum flow by hotend and material Every hotend has a flow ceiling, set by heater power, melt-zone length and nozzle geometry. When you exceed it, the extruder cannot push the plastic through; you see under-extrusion, matte rough lines, skipped steps or the extruder clicking. Typical ranges for a 0.4 mm nozzle follow. Treat them as starting points, not guarantees and measure your own (see max volumetric speed test ). Hotend class PLA PETG ABS / ASA PA / PC TPU Basic, long-melt-zone hotend (older/budget printers) 8–12 6–10 7–11 5–9 2–4 Modern standard hotend 15–25 10–16 12–20 8–14 3–8 High-flow / high-power hotend 25–40 14–25 18–30 12–20 5–10 Values in mm³/s. Actual limits vary with brand, nozzle temperature, line width and how well the filament is dried. Typical maximum flow (mm³/s) for a modern standard hotend PLA 15–25 PETG 10–16 ABS / ASA 12–20 PA / PC 8–14 TPU 3–8 🔧 What speed does a flow limit allow? Assume a 0.42 mm line and 15 mm³/s limit. The fastest sustainable print speed by layer height: Layer height Area w × h Max speed at 15 mm³/s At 25 mm³/s 0.08 mm 0.034 mm² ≈ 446 mm/s ≈ 744 mm/s 0.12 mm 0.050 mm² ≈ 298 mm/s ≈ 496 mm/s 0.16 mm 0.067 mm² ≈ 223 mm/s ≈ 372 mm/s 0.20 mm 0.084 mm² ≈ 179 mm/s ≈ 298 mm/s 0.28 mm 0.118 mm² ≈ 128 mm/s ≈ 213 mm/s The values are theoretical top speeds on straight lines; real walls are short, so acceleration (next section) is usually the true limiter. But for infill and long walls, flow rules. Practical rule Set the filament's max volumetric speed in your slicer to a tested value (about 80–90 % of the failure point). The slicer then slows lines automatically when a thick, wide line would exceed it, so you can leave your speed settings high and let the flow cap protect quality. Common mistake Setting a sky-high speed and wondering why the part looks under-extruded. The printer might simply be asked to melt 40 mm³/s through a 15 mm³/s hotend. Compute flow (width × height × speed) before blaming the filament. 🚀 Raising the flow limit Raise nozzle temperature by 10–20 °C: hotter plastic flows easier and melts faster. Compensate with stronger cooling. Use a high-flow hotend or a longer melt zone (volcano-style, dual heater, ceramic/high-power heater). Use a bigger nozzle (0.6 mm): the same speed gives 2–2.5× the flow, at the cost of fine detail. Dry the filament. Wet filament boils in the nozzle, steam bubbles reduce throughput and quality; see drying & storage . Use a good extruder. Strong dual-gear direct-drive extruders keep grip at high pressure. See printer anatomy . Bambu X2D The X2D's main (left) nozzle uses a direct-drive servo extruder, while the auxiliary (right) nozzle is fed by a stepper-driven extruder at the rear and has lower speed and acceleration limits (around 200 mm/s and ~1,000 mm/s² per Bambu's documentation). In practice this means choosing your speed per nozzle: the aux nozzle is for supports and secondary materials, not for race-pace infill. See dual-nozzle printing . Acceleration and jerk 🔰 Why top speed is not the whole story Acceleration (mm/s²) is how quickly the toolhead changes speed. A part is full of corners, short walls and travel moves, so the toolhead is constantly speeding up and slowing down. x: Multi-color & multi-material · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques Multi-color & multi-material Print in several colors or several plastics in one job. Learn the hardware approaches, why color changes create waste, how to shrink that waste, and how to design models that look great in color without hours of purging. Intermediate ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn Five ways to print with more than one filament, what happens inside the nozzle during a change, how prime towers and flush volumes work, how to cut waste, how to design for color, which materials stick to each other, and the usual AMS-style pitfalls and how to avoid them. 🔰 Five ways to print in more than one filament A single-nozzle printer has one melt zone and one nozzle, so changing filament means getting one plastic out and the next in. Different machines solve that problem in different ways, each with its own strengths and costs. Figure 1. Five hardware approaches. They differ in where filament is switched: before the nozzle (swap, feeder), at the toolhead (toolchanger, dual nozzle) or inside the melt zone (mixing). 1. Filament swaps (M600 and pause-at-layer) The simplest method: tell the slicer to pause at a certain layer. The printer parks, you unload the old filament, load the new one, purge a short length until the new color flows cleanly, and resume. The G-code commonly used is M600 (filament change), though some firmware calls it a pause plus a macro. It needs no extra hardware and wastes only a few centimeters of filament, which makes it ideal for stripes and layers of color such as lithophanes, name plates, and a color change halfway up a vase. The drawback is that you must be at the printer, and every change adds a manual step. 2. Multi-spool feeders (AMS-style systems) A feeder holds several spools and pushes the chosen filament through a tube to a single extruder. The system retracts the old filament out of the hotend (often into a buffer or back to the feeder) and loads the new one automatically. It can do hundreds of changes per print with no human help. Because there is still one nozzle, every change must flush the old color out of the melt zone before the new color is clean, and that creates waste (see waste mechanics ). Examples include Bambu's AMS family, Prusa's MMU, Creality's CFS and similar systems. 3. Toolchangers A toolchanger parks several complete toolheads on a rack. To change colors the gantry puts one head down and picks up another. Because each head carries its own nozzle and its own filament, there is nothing to purge from the melt zone; at most you wipe the nozzle on a small tower to remove ooze. The result is very low waste , and a toolchanger can combine very different materials (for example PLA and PETG with different temperatures). Costs are mechanical complexity, alignment between heads (offsets must be calibrated to a fraction of a millimeter), and heads that idle at a standby temperature and leak. 4. Dual-nozzle and multi-nozzle toolheads Two nozzles share one carriage; the active one lowers while the idle one is lifted (or both sit at fixed offsets and the slicer plans around their positions). Each nozzle can hold a different filament, so for two-color or model-plus-support prints almost no purging is needed. A dual-nozzle machine with an AMS-style feeder on each side can do both: print fast with minimal waste while still reaching many colors. The nozzles have a fixed offset, so the build area for a given nozzle may be smaller than the full bed. Bambu X2D The X2D is a dual-nozzle printer designed to cut the purge needed for two-filament jobs. The two nozzles are not identical in role, so how a model is split between them matters; read Dual-nozzle printing for the limits and strategies. 5. Mixing hotends and gradient printing A mixing hotend feeds two, three or more filaments into one melt chamber, where they blend before leaving the nozzle. By changing the ratio per layer you get gradients; by changing it quickly you get marbled or "tweed" effects. Colors are never crisp because the chamber holds a pool of the previous mix, and not many printers use this today. It is a fun niche for rainbow vases. Painting versus assigning Some slicers let you paint colors directly onto the model surface, while others only let you assign a filament to an entire object or part. The hardware method decides how many colors you can reach; the slicer's tools decide how comfortable it is to use them. Both are covered below. Purge, flush and the waste problem 🔰 What actually happens during a color change When a single-nozzle printer swaps filaments, the melted old plastic is still inside the nozzle and melt zone. If the new filament is pushed in, the first segment of extrusion will be a blend of old and new colors. Three jobs have to be done before printing resumes with a clean new color: Retract and unload The old filament is pulled up out of the melt zone, often with a cooling-and-tip-shaping routine so it does not leave strings or blobs in the extruder. Load and push The new filament is fed down to the extruder gears and pushed into the melt zone, shoving the remaining old melt out of the nozzle. Flush The printer extrudes extra filament (the flush volume ) until the output is clean new color. This material is thrown away or hidden in a purge area. Flush volume is typically in the hundreds of cubic millimeters per change, but it depends strongly on the colors involved, as seen below. Figure 2. The nozzle and melt zone hold a small reservoir of old color. Flushing replaces it with new color; the blend in between has to go somewhere. The prime (wipe) tower The usual dumping ground is a prime tower (also called a wipe tower): a thin rectangular stack printed beside the model. At each color change the nozzle moves to the tower, flushes there, and then lays down a few tower layers in the new color to condition the nozzle before returning to the model. x: Calibration playbook · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques Calibration playbook Calibration turns a printer that merely works into one that is predictable. Follow the order of operations, use the right test model for each step, learn what good and bad results look like, and record the numbers so you never repeat work. Intermediate ⏱ 45 min read What you will learn Why order matters, how to check the machine itself, how to tune bed, Z-offset, temperature, flow, pressure advance, retraction, volumetric speed, cooling, dimensions and input shaping, how to apply each result, how to manage per-filament profiles and when to repeat tests. A printable calibration log is at the end. 🔰 Order of operations Calibration steps depend on each other. If you tune flow before the temperature is right, the flow number is wrong after you change temperature. If you tune pressure advance on a loose belt, the pattern is smeared by mechanics, not by plastic. The rule is simple: fix the physical machine first, then first layer, then plastic behavior, then speed and motion. Figure 1. The calibration order. Left column: machine and first layer. Middle: material behavior. Right: speed, cooling, accuracy and motion. Not every printer needs every step Bambu printers (and other enclosed, self-calibrating machines) perform steps 3, 4, 7 and 12 automatically; you should still understand them and know when to trigger a manual run. See Bambu automatic calibration . Other machines may need you to do them by hand. 1–2 · Mechanical check, belts and frame 🔰 Do this before touching the slicer No software setting repairs a loose machine. Spend ten minutes on the hardware: Frame: All visible screws snug, no wobble when you push the frame gently. The printer stands on a solid, level surface. Axes move smoothly: Power off, move the toolhead and bed by hand (where safe). There should be no gritty spots, binding or loud knocks. Belts: Equal tension, no frayed edges, teeth meshing with the pulleys. A plucked belt gives a clear tone (see belts & vibrations ). Nozzle and hotend: Nozzle seated and tight (when hot, per the manufacturer's procedure), no filament leaking around it, fan ducts attached. Extruder: Gears clean, no filament dust build-up, tension correct, filament path free of kinks. Bed and plate: Plate clean, flat and seated properly, with no debris beneath. Squareness: If your printer allows, check that X and Y are square with a printed square or by measuring diagonals (they should be equal within a few tenths of a millimeter). Figure 2. Simple geometry tests reveal frame skew and axis scale errors before you tune anything else. 🚀 Steps per millimeter, e-steps and rotation distance Firmware needs to know how far each motor moves per command. For axes this is set by belt pitch, pulley teeth and microstepping, and is almost always right by default. For the extruder it depends on the gear, so a wrong value means every flow calculation is off. E-steps (Marlin) = steps per mm of filament. Rotation distance (Klipper) = mm of filament per motor revolution. Test: Mark the filament 120 mm above the extruder entrance, command a 100 mm extrusion (hot, slowly, e.g. 50 mm/min), and measure what remains. If 100 mm was requested but only 97 mm moved, the new value is: new e-steps = old × 100 / 97 . In Klipper: new rotation distance = old × actual / requested . Do it once per extruder (and after replacing the gears), not for each filament. Differences between filaments belong to flow rate . Printers with firmware and extruders from the manufacturer (including sealed, enclosed models) usually do not expose or need this step. The same idea applies to motor current and thermal safety: do not raise motor current beyond what the driver and motor allow just to hide a mechanical issue. 🚀 PID tuning concept The hotend and bed heaters are controlled by a loop that decides how much power to apply based on the difference between the target and the measured temperature. PID stands for proportional, integral and derivative: P reacts to the current error, I corrects accumulated error, D anticipates change. Badly tuned PID causes temperature to oscillate by several degrees, which shows up as periodic changes in surface gloss or flow, and sometimes as thermal-runaway errors. Figure 3. PID tuning aims for a quick rise with little overshoot. Most firmware has an auto-tune command that runs heating cycles at a set temperature and stores new constants. Run auto-tune at the temperature you use most (nozzle at a typical print temperature, bed at your usual bed temperature) with the part-cooling fan at its usual speed. Repeat it after replacing a heater, thermistor or hotend, or when the temperature graph wiggles visibly. 3 · Bed leveling and mesh The goal is a constant distance from nozzle to bed everywhere. Two things matter: the bed's tram (is the gantry parallel to the bed?) and its flatness (is the plate itself warped?). Manual tramming: Adjust screws with a paper or feeler gauge at the four corners and center; repeat once since screws interact. Use the same bed temperature as printing; the bed bends when hot. Automatic mesh: A probe measures a grid of points (for example 7×7), and firmware compensates by raising or lowering Z during the first layers. Make sure the mesh is made hot and with a clean nozzle. Mesh cannot hide a tilt. A tilted gantry or bed should be corrected mechanically first: otherwise the mesh has to correct large errors that fade with height and distort the first layers. Figure 4. Mesh heat maps. A flat plate shows a pale, uniform map; a bowl or tilted plate shows strong color gradients. 4 · Z-offset Z-offset sets the nozzle's height above the bed at the first layer. Too high and lines do not stick; too low and they are squashed, and the nozzle may scratch the plate. Detailed squish diagrams are in First layer & bed adhesion ; the short version: Test model Print a single-layer large square (for example 150×150 mm) or a grid of 5 pat

x: Advanced techniques · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques Advanced techniques Once a printer prints reliably, the interesting part begins: tricks that make parts faster, stronger, prettier, smarter or simply impossible to make any other way. This page is a toolbox of more than thirty techniques, each with when to use it, how to do it, and what can go wrong. Advanced ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn How to pick the right special technique for a job, set it up in any slicer, and avoid its typical failure modes. Every technique below follows the same pattern: When to use it → How → Caveats , usually with a diagram. You should be comfortable with calibration , supports and slicer settings before you start. The technique map Advanced techniques fall into a handful of families. Knowing the family tells you which part of the process you are changing: the toolpath (what the nozzle does), the geometry (what you model), the material (what goes in), or the workflow (what happens around the print). Figure 1. Four families of advanced technique. Most real projects combine two or three of them. Technique Main benefit Difficulty Typical cost Vase / spiral mode Fast, leak-free single-wall shells Easy None Variable layer height Smooth curves without long print times Easy None Ironing Mirror-flat top surfaces Medium Extra time Fuzzy skin Grip texture, hides layer lines Easy None Modifiers / per-region settings Strength or speed only where needed Medium None Print-in-place mechanisms Assembled moving parts from one job Hard Test prints Embedded hardware Threads, magnets, weights, electronics Medium Hardware Lithophanes Photos in relief that glow when backlit Medium Light source Lattice / TPMS Light, tunable, energy-absorbing parts Hard Software Casting & molds Metal, silicone or resin copies of prints Hard Materials Batch production Many parts per day Medium Time, printers Part A · Toolpath techniques 🔰 Vase mode (spiral contour) Vase mode (Cura calls it Spiralize outer contour , Bambu Studio and Orca call it Spiral vase ) prints a single continuous wall that rises slowly with every revolution. The nozzle never lifts, never retracts and never leaves a seam, because the Z height increases smoothly along the path instead of in discrete steps. Figure 2. In vase mode the contour climbs by one layer height per revolution. The base is printed solid; everything above is a single wall. When to use it Vases, cups, lampshades, planters, desk organizers: anything that is a smooth, open-top shell. Fast, watertight containers (a single continuous wall has no seam to leak through). Translucent lamp shades: wall thickness is uniform, so light glows evenly. Material tests: a single-wall vase quickly shows stringing, cooling and temperature behavior. How Choose a model that works A closed outer surface, no internal walls, no overhangs steeper than your printer tolerates. Anything that needs a second perimeter in the same layer cannot be printed. Enable spiral mode Turn on Spiral vase . Set top solid layers to 0 (there is no lid) and bottom layers to 3–5 so the base is watertight. Sparse infill is ignored. Pick a wide nozzle line Wall thickness equals the extrusion width. A 0.4 mm nozzle with a 0.45–0.6 mm line gives a thin, flexible wall; a 0.8 mm nozzle gives a sturdy 0.8–1.0 mm wall and prints faster. Raise flow and lower speed slightly Because there is no overlap with neighboring walls, flow errors show immediately. Start at 100 % flow and compare wall thickness with calipers; a 3 % change is already visible. Print it Use a brim for tall, narrow shapes. Remove the finished object by twisting gently; the thin base can crack otherwise. Caveats Single wall = weak in Z Every layer is bonded only to the one below it by a thin strip of plastic. Vase-mode parts are stiff around the circumference but can split along layers when squeezed or dropped. Use higher nozzle temperature (+5–10 °C) and a slightly slower speed for better layer bonding. For parts that must hold liquid and take abuse, add 2 perimeters instead (a normal print). Pro trick: patterned vases Because the wall height changes continuously, you can twist, ripple or wave the model's outline in CAD. The seamless path makes these shapes look stunning in silk or translucent filaments. Dual-color filament gradients (see gradients ) turn a plain vase into a showpiece. 🔰 Variable (adaptive) layer height Layer height is a trade between speed and surface quality. Variable layer height lets the slicer use thin layers where the shape curves slowly (shoulders, domes, tilted faces) and thick layers on vertical walls , where thickness hardly affects the look. A 200 mm tall bust may drop from 12 hours to 8 hours with almost no visible loss. Figure 3. Stair-stepping error is largest where the surface is almost horizontal. Variable layer height puts the fine layers only there. How Automatic: Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer, PrusaSlicer and Cura (via the Adaptive layers option or experimental setting) have a smoothing slider that trades quality against time. Start at the middle value and preview the layer-height color map. Manual: Paint a layer-height profile or use a height range modifier (see modifiers ) to say “from Z = 40 to 60 mm use 0.08 mm”. Ideal for a face, a logo or a threaded section. Sensible limits: keep layer height between 20 % and 75 % of the nozzle diameter, and stay within what your cooling can handle. Caveats Z-axis speed and extrusion pressure must cope with sudden layer height changes; use a smoothing value of at least medium. Thicker layers cool slower; very thin layers heat up the previous layer. Watch for blobs on tiny features. Layer adhesion varies: thin layers bond better than thick ones, so do not use extremes on functional load-bearing walls. Pressure advance and flow calibrations done at 0.20 mm are still good for 0.12–0.28 mm in most cases; recalibrate for extremes. 🔧 Ironing Ironing makes a final pass over each top surface with the hot nozzle moving s

x: Post-processing · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques Post-processing A print coming off the plate is a raw part. Post-processing is everything after: removing supports, sanding, filling, painting, smoothing, strengthening, joining and installing hardware. This page walks the whole ladder from “good enough” to “is that really 3D printed?”. Intermediate ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn Which finish to aim for (and how long it takes), how to remove supports cleanly, how to sand and prime properly, how to smooth, coat and paint, how to anneal for strength and heat resistance, how to glue and weld plastics, and how to install inserts, threads and magnets. Safety notes are included wherever a chemical or tool can hurt you. Choose your finish level first Post-processing time grows faster than quality. The first minutes give big gains; the last 5 % of perfection can take hours. Decide your target before you start, so you do not over-polish a functional bracket or under-finish a display piece. Figure 1. The finish ladder: quality rises quickly at first, then slowly. Pick the lowest level that meets the purpose. Figure 2. A typical sequence. The dashed loop is the most common one: sand, prime, inspect, repeat. Why order matters Annealing and gluing change shape or add seams, so do them before sanding and painting. Paint and clear coat should come last because they can soften or contaminate surfaces that you still need to glue. Heat-set inserts go in before painting so a slipped iron does not scar the finish. 1 · Support removal and cleanup 🔰 Removing supports safely Let the plate cool Most parts release more cleanly when cool (below ~30 °C) because the plastic is stiffer and the bed contraction frees the first layer. Parts on textured PEI plates often pop off after a minute. Start from the outside in Grip the support near its base with pliers or your fingers and bend away from the model, not toward it. Peel in the direction that pulls the support off the surface rather than pushes it into it. Use flush cutters for stubborn bits Cut each support strut close to the surface, then remove the stub with a sharp craft knife or by sanding. Always cut away from your body and wear eye protection: small plastic fragments fly. Clean the interface Remove leftover interface layers with a deburring tool or a fine file. Smooth bumps with 180–240 grit sandpaper. Safety Never pull a blade toward your hand. Use a cut-resistant glove on the holding hand when cutting thick supports, and place the part on a non-slip mat. Eye protection is mandatory when snipping brittle materials such as PLA or PLA-CF. Hand tools worth owning 🔧 Flush cutters Trim supports, strings and filament ends cleanly. One flat side leaves almost no stub. 🔪 Hobby knife + deburring tool Scrape elephant foot, brims and seam bulges. Rotating deburr blades work best for edges. 🧰 Needle-nose pliers Grip support roots. Long tweezers retrieve small bits inside cavities. 📏 Needle files Clean holes, slots and sharp corners; round files fix undersized holes. 🧽 Sanding sponges and sticks Foam-backed blocks follow curves; flat sticks keep edges crisp. 🌬️ Compressed air / soft brush Dust control. Keeps dust off wet paint and out of the printer. 🔧 Other support types Soluble supports (PVA, BVOH): soak the part in room-temperature water for hours; stir occasionally and refresh the water. PVA is slow and smells when dissolving; BVOH dissolves faster. Dry the part afterwards before painting or sealing. Breakaway supports: special filaments with a weak bond. Peel by hand; use the matching interface material recommended by the filament maker. Dual-nozzle supports: on the Bambu X2D the auxiliary nozzle can lay down support in a different material so the interface peels off easily; see dual-nozzle printing and supports . Fixing small defects before sanding Defect Quick fix Strings and hairs Brush with a toothbrush, then pass a heat gun for one second at a distance (PLA) or flick with a lighter only if the material is non-sticky. Keep flames away from the part. Blobs and zits Scrape with a sharp blade at a shallow angle, then sand with 220 grit. Elephant foot File or sand the bottom 1 mm with 120 grit on a flat block. Brim remnants Peel the brim; trim the edge with a deburring tool. Z-seam line Sand across the seam with 220 grit; fill with putty if deep. Cracks along layers Fill with CA glue and baking soda, then sand. Consider printing hotter next time. 2 · Sanding Sanding turns layer lines into a smooth surface by abrading plastic away. The trick is to work through grits in order, never skipping more than one step. Each grit removes the scratches of the previous one and leaves finer ones. Figure 3. What sanding does to a surface. Each stage removes the scratches of the previous grit. Grit progression table Stage Grit (US/CAMI P) Purpose Wet or dry Remarks Rough shaping 80–120 Remove seams, stubs, big layer ridges Dry Use a block; do not stay in one spot or it will melt Smoothing 180–240 Remove 120 scratches, level the surface Dry Main stage for most prints Pre-primer 320–400 Even matte surface Dry or wet Good enough for filler primer Between primer coats 400–600 Level primer, remove dust nibs Wet Light pressure only Pre-paint 600–800 Silky base for paint Wet Wipe clean, tack cloth Clear-coat polish 1000–2000+ Remove orange peel and dust Wet Then polishing compound Technique Wet sanding (with a few drops of dish soap in water) reduces dust, prevents clogging and keeps plastic cool. Use waterproof paper from 400 grit up. Dry sanding is fine for coarse grits, but dust from CF, GF or glass-bead filaments is hazardous: wear a P2/FFP2 respirator. Use backing: sand over a flat block for flat faces, a sponge for curves, folded paper for tight spots. Cross-hatch strokes (alternate 90° directions) so you can see when old scratches are gone. x: Troubleshooting gallery · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques Troubleshooting gallery Forty illustrated defects, each with a picture of what you are looking at, the causes ranked from most to least likely, step-by-step fixes and prevention. Use the symptom picker, the decision tree, or just scroll the gallery. Beginner → Expert ⏱ 45 min read · reference How to use this page 1) Run the first five checks , which fix more than half of all failures. 2) Find your symptom with the symptom picker or the decision tree . 3) Work through the causes in the order listed and change one thing at a time . 4) Log what worked. Settings names follow Bambu Studio/OrcaSlicer; PrusaSlicer and Cura use near-identical terms. For X2D-specific parts, see X2D maintenance & troubleshooting . The first five checks for any failure Most printing problems come from a short list of root causes. Before you tune a single setting, run through this list. It takes five minutes and saves hours of chasing symptoms. 1 · The first layer. Is it squished evenly, with lines touching and no gaps or ridges? Is the plate clean (wipe with IPA, or warm water and dish soap, no finger oils)? See first layer & adhesion . 2 · The filament. Is it dry and the right type in the right profile? Popping, hissing, fuzzy surfaces and stringing mean wet filament. See drying & storage . 3 · The filament path. Does the spool unwind freely, with no tangles, kinks or sharp bends? Is the extruder gripping with no grinding and no clicking? 4 · The nozzle. Is it clean (no burnt crust), the right size, tightened, and flowing a smooth, straight strand when you extrude by hand? Compare the flow to a fresh nozzle. 5 · The profile. Are temperature, cooling and speed set for this material and layer height? Is volumetric flow within the hotend’s limit? See speed, cooling & quality . The golden rule Change one variable, print a small test (a 20 mm cube or a calibration tower takes 10–20 minutes), compare, and keep notes. Changing five things at once turns troubleshooting into guessing. Diagnostic decision tree Start at the top. Pick the column that matches when and where the problem appears; each box links to the matching card in the gallery. Figure 1. A four-branch decision tree. If two branches fit, start with the one that appeared earliest in the print. Figure 2. When each class of problem typically shows up. Symptom picker and defect gallery Filter by category or type a word ( strings, gaps, rough, clicking, color… ) to narrow the gallery. Cards are listed within their category; each card shows a schematic (not a photo) of what to look for, then causes in descending likelihood. 🔎 Symptom picker All Extrusion & flow Adhesion & warping Layers & structure Surface & dimensions Motion & vibration Overhangs & supports Multi-material & AMS No defect matches. Try a broader word such as “gaps”, “rough”, “weak” or “noise”, or reset the category to “All”. 🟠 Extrusion & flow 1 · Stringing hairs between parts Look for: thin hairs or cobwebs across open spaces after the nozzle travels. Causes (most likely first) Wet filament (steam pushes plastic out during travel) Nozzle temperature too high Retraction too short or off, or travel too slow Slow travel speed / wiping disabled Material is naturally stringy (PETG, TPU) Fix Dry the filament (PLA 45–55 °C for 6–8 h; PETG 60–65 °C for 6–8 h). Lower nozzle temperature in 5 °C steps until stringing fades but layer bonding stays good. Increase retraction in small steps (direct drive: 0.4–1.0 mm; Bowden: 2–5 mm). Enable wipe on retract and avoid crossing open areas. Raise travel speed (150–300 mm/s); run a retraction test tower. Prevention: store filament sealed or in a dry box; use a calibrated profile per filament. 2 · Oozing / drooling plastic leaks from a resting nozzle Look for: blobs on the surface, a thin line of plastic at the start of moves, a drip on the bed. Causes Wet filament or too-hot nozzle (pressure remains in the melt chamber) Retraction disabled or too small Waiting on a hot nozzle (heat soak, filament changes) Worn or loose nozzle (leak around the thread) Fix Dry filament; lower temperature 5–10 °C. Increase retraction, enable wipe and “retract on layer change”. Keep waiting times short, or retract before long pauses. Hot-tighten the nozzle (see maintenance ) or replace it. Prevention: use a purge/wipe move before printing and avoid keeping the nozzle hot while idle. 3 · Blobs and zits small bumps on the wall Look for: pimples at the same spot every layer (seam) or random dots. Causes Pressure not released at layer start/end (retraction, pressure advance too low) Over-extrusion or temperature too high Seam position set to “nearest” or “random” on a visible face Wet filament or dirty nozzle Fix Calibrate pressure advance/flow dynamics, then flow ratio. Set seam to “aligned” or “back” and hide it at a sharp edge; use scarf seam if available. Enable “wipe before outer wall” and reduce temperature 5 °C. Dry filament; clean the nozzle. Prevention: run the calibration sequence whenever you change filament. 4 · Under-extrusion not enough plastic Look for: thin, gappy or missing lines, weak parts, rough infill, dotted lines in the first layer. Causes Partial clog or worn nozzle Nozzle too cold or speed too high for volumetric flow limit Wet or bad-quality filament; wrong diameter Extruder tension/gear dirt or filament path friction Flow ratio too low Fix Do a cold pull ( procedure below ) or replace the nozzle. Raise temperature 5–10 °C or lower max volumetric speed to the filament’s limit. Dry filament; measure its diameter in three places. Clean the extruder gear and check feed tension; remove tight bends. Re-run flow calibration. Prevention: replace nozzles on schedule and keep filament dry. 5 · Over-extrusion too much plastic Look for: parts larger than designed, rough or bumpy walls, filled corners, ridged top surfaces. x: Printer maintenance · 3D Printing Compendium Part 4 · Techniques Printer maintenance A 3D printer is a small robot that heats plastic to 250 °C, moves a toolhead at hundreds of millimeters per second and runs for hours unattended. Fifteen minutes of care a week keeps it accurate, quiet and safe. This page is a generic schedule that fits almost any FDM machine; the X2D-specific steps live on a dedicated page. Beginner ⏱ 35 min read What you will learn What to do after every print, weekly, monthly, quarterly and yearly; how to clean and lubricate correctly (and what not to lubricate); how to judge belt tension, wear and consumable life; how to store or ship a printer; and how to keep a log so you catch problems early. Using a Bambu Lab X2D? This page stays generic on purpose. For the X2D procedures (dual-nozzle hotends, auxiliary extruder, AMS 2 Pro, carbon filter, cutter) see X2D maintenance & troubleshooting . The principles below still apply. Power off and cool down first Switch the printer off and unplug it before touching wiring, the toolhead board, heater cartridges or thermistors. Let the nozzle and bed cool below 40 °C before working near them. A short circuit from a loose wire can destroy the mainboard; a 250 °C nozzle gives instant burns. Why maintenance matters Most print failures are not mysterious. They are the visible end of slow wear: a nozzle slowly partially clogged, a belt that has lost tension, a fan full of dust, a plate that is greasy from fingerprints. Preventive maintenance has three payoffs: Quality. Clean rails and tight belts give smooth walls, accurate dimensions and fewer ringing marks. Reliability. You find a frayed cable or a worn gear when it is a ten-minute fix instead of a failed overnight print. Safety and cost. Dust on heaters, loose terminals and worn insulation are fire risks. Replacing a $10 part on schedule is cheaper than replacing a $200 hotend. The routine schedule Intervals depend on how much you print. The table assumes a typical hobby load of 5–20 hours a week. Printing abrasive or dusty materials (carbon-fiber or glass-fiber filled, glow-in-the-dark) or high-temperature enclosures shortens everything by roughly half. If the printer sits idle for a month, you still need the monthly rail check, but you can skip belt and gear work. A simple rule: do a mini-service every 200 printing hours . Figure 1. A visual year. Pin a copy near the printer or put reminders in your phone calendar: weekly on a fixed day, monthly on the 1st, quarterly with the season. Cleaning: nozzle, bed and build plate Build plate Skin oil, hand cream and dust are the number one reason a perfectly calibrated first layer fails. Clean the plate in two steps: warm water with a drop of dish soap (removes grease), rinse and dry with a lint-free towel, then wipe with isopropyl alcohol (70–99 %) if the manufacturer allows it. Never touch the print surface with bare fingers; hold the plate by its edge. Smooth PEI: washes well; a light Scotch-Brite pad can restore bite once in a while. Nozzle and hotend exterior With the nozzle at printing temperature (and the printer powered normally), use brass-brush or tweezers to remove burnt plastic from the tip. x: Design principles (DfAM) · 3D Printing Compendium Part 5 · Design for printing Design principles (DfAM) A part that looks perfect on screen can still fail on the bed. Learn the handful of physical rules behind every FDM print and design parts that print first time, strong, and without a forest of supports. Beginner → Intermediate ⏱ 35 min read What you will learn How to think like an additive manufacturing designer: choose wall thicknesses that match the extrusion width, respect minimum feature sizes, keep overhangs under control, orient parts on purpose, and review a design with a checklist before you press “Print”. All numbers assume a 0.4 mm nozzle , 0.2 mm layers and a typical FDM printer such as the Bambu Lab X2D; scale them for other nozzles with the table further down. 🔰 The DfAM mindset Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM) means shaping a part around the way a machine actually builds it. A CNC mill removes material with a spinning tool, an injection mold fills a cavity, and an FDM printer draws a stack of thin plastic lines, one layer on top of another . Every rule in this chapter is a consequence of that one sentence. FDM gives you real freedoms: internal cavities, organic shapes, part consolidation, no tooling cost, one-off geometry at the same price as the tenth copy. It also imposes constraints that traditional manufacturing does not have: nothing can be printed in mid-air, layer-to-layer bonds are weaker than the plastic itself, the smallest feature is limited by a nozzle opening of 0.4 mm, and the first layer must sit flat on a plate. Figure 1. A wall is a stack of round-edged extrusion lines. Layer height is the vertical step, line width the horizontal one. Every DfAM rule starts from these two numbers. The three kinds of constraint Geometric – overhangs, bridges, minimum feature size, and the need for a flat contact face (this chapter). Mechanical – the part is anisotropic: strong along the lines, weaker between layers (see Strength & orientation ). Dimensional – plastic shrinks and squishes, so a 10.00 mm hole prints as 9.7 mm (see Tolerances & fits ). 🏆 The 10 golden rules If you only remember ten sentences from this site, make them these. Each rule is expanded in its own section below. Figure 2. The ten golden rules and the order in which to apply them: function → orientation → geometry → test. Give the part a flat base. A large flat face on the plate is the most important adhesion and accuracy feature you can design in. Round or pointed bottoms need a flat cut or a raft. Respect the 45° rule. Surfaces leaning outward by up to about 45° from vertical print well. Between 45° and 60° the underside gets rough; beyond about 60° you need support or a redesign. Make walls multiples of the line width. With 0.45 mm lines use 0.9, 1.35, 1.8 or 2.25 mm walls so the slicer fills them with whole lines instead of tiny gap-fill slivers. Orient for strength. The layer interface is the weak link. Arrange parts so that loads run along the layers, not across them. Add fillets inside, chamfers at the bed. Inner radii spread stress; a 0.4–0.6 mm chamfer on the first-layer edge hides elephant foot. Keep bridges short. A bridge is plastic stretched through air. Under about 10 mm it is almost always fine; 30 mm is typically the upper limit with tuned cooling. Plan for holes to shrink. Round holes come out 0.1–0.3 mm too small. Model them oversize and verify with a test coupon. Avoid thin, tall features. The nozzle pushes and vibrates them. Keep height to width at or below 5 : 1, taper them, or brace them. Split instead of supporting. Two flat-bottomed halves with dowels usually beat one part full of support scars. Test small first. A 10-minute slice of the tricky region saves a 10-hour failure. 🔰 Wall thickness: think in line widths The slicer fills the volume of your model with perimeters (outlines) and infill . A wall is built from whole perimeter lines. Each line is about 0.42–0.45 mm wide for a 0.4 mm nozzle (the extruded bead is slightly wider than the opening because it is squished against the layer below). A wall that is a whole multiple of that width is filled with clean, continuous lines; a wall that is not will show gaps, over-extrusion bulges or noisy zig-zag “gap fill” strokes. Figure 3. Top-down slices through a wall. Whole-line walls fill cleanly; a 1.0 mm wall leaves a remainder the slicer must improvise on. Modern slicers (Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer) vary line width on the fly, which hides the issue, but whole multiples still give the strongest and most predictable result. Perimeters Wall thickness (0.45 mm lines) Typical use 1 0.45 mm Vase mode, decorative shells, thin lids. Fragile. 2 0.9 mm Light covers, organizers, miniatures. Practical minimum. 3 1.35 mm General functional parts, enclosures. 4 1.8 mm Snap-fit hooks, screw bosses, brackets. 5–6 2.25–2.7 mm Highly loaded parts, threads, pressure-bearing walls. Rule of thumb For a structural part, set the slicer to 3–4 walls and design walls at 1.35–1.8 mm . Beyond about six walls extra strength comes mainly from infill and geometry, not from more perimeters (see Strength & orientation ). Why it works Each perimeter is bonded to its neighbors sideways while the previous layer is still warm, and to the layer below, so the outer 2–3 lines carry most bending and torsion loads. Stiffness of a thin wall grows with the cube of its thickness, so going from 0.9 mm to 1.35 mm roughly triples bending stiffness (1.5³ ≈ 3.4). 🔰 Minimum feature sizes A feature smaller than the line width simply cannot exist, and a feature only slightly larger is unreliable. The table lists realistic minimums for a 0.4 mm nozzle with 0.2 mm layers. “Reliable” means it prints correctly almost every time; “possible” means it needs tuning or luck. Feature Possible Reliable Notes Free-standing wall (thickness) 0.45 mm 0.9 mm+ Single-line walls are weak sideways. x: Tolerances & fits · 3D Printing Compendium Part 5 · Design for printing Tolerances & fits Why a 10 mm hole prints at 9.7 mm, how much clearance every kind of fit needs, and how to calibrate your printer so the parts you design actually go together on the first try. Intermediate ⏱ 40 min read What you will learn Where dimensional errors come from, how to choose clearance for press, snug, slip, sliding and print-in-place fits, how to design and print a tolerance test coupon, how to set up CAD parameters so a one-number change adapts a design to a new printer or filament, and how to compute recommended hole sizes with the calculator on this page. All values assume a 0.4 mm nozzle and 0.2 mm layers ; they are starting points that you must verify with your own printer. 🔰 Where dimensional errors come from Tolerance is the permitted deviation from a nominal size. A machinist working with a lathe expects ±0.01 mm; a typical FDM printer delivers roughly ±0.1–0.3 mm on small features and about ±0.5 % on larger ones. The good news is that most of the error is systematic , meaning it is the same every time, so you can measure it once and design around it. Truly random error is much smaller. Figure 1. The five places where a printed dimension can drift from the model. Calibration removes the systematic part; clearance covers the random part. 🔰 Shrinkage and horizontal expansion Two different effects change sizes in the XY plane, and they push in opposite directions on different features: Thermal shrinkage – plastic extruded at 200–280 °C contracts as it cools to room temperature. Every dimension scales by (1 − shrinkage). PLA shrinks only 0.2–0.5 %; nylon and ABS shrink more and also warp. Horizontal expansion (squish) – the bead is wider than its nominal line width and is pressed outward by the nozzle. The outer perimeter ends up slightly outside the CAD outline, and the inner perimeter of a hole slightly inside it, so outside dimensions grow and holes shrink. Figure 2. Left: outside surfaces grow while holes shrink, so the same offset must be applied with opposite signs. Right: cooling shrinkage scales with the dimension, which is why large parts need a bigger correction than small ones. Why holes print small Slicers approximate a circle with a polygon whose corners lie on the circle, so the polygon’s sides lie inside it. In addition, the inner perimeter bead is pressed inward by the plastic’s own flow and surface tension. Both effects reduce the hole and both scale weakly with diameter, so a 3 mm hole typically loses 0.15–0.25 mm while a 30 mm hole loses roughly 0.2–0.3 mm. 🔰 Clearance tables: from press fit to loose A fit describes how two mating parts relate: a shaft (the male feature: pin, rod, boss) goes into a hole (the female feature). Clearance is hole minus shaft; a negative number is an interference (press fit). The numbers below are diametral CAD clearance : the hole diameter in the model minus the shaft diameter in the model, for a well-tuned 0.4 mm printer printing PLA or PETG with the axis vertical. Add more for large diameters, horizontal axes or high-shrink materials, and subtract for very well-calibrated machines. Fit class CAD clearance (diametral) Behavior Typical use Press fit 0.00 to +0.10 mm Needs a hammer or vise; permanent. Dowel pins, bushings, magnets, bearings in a tight seat. Snug / transition +0.10 to +0.20 mm Hand push, holds without glue. Lid plugs, alignment pins, inserts with glue. Slip fit +0.20 to +0.30 mm Slides by hand with slight resistance, no wobble. Stack-up parts, slide-on caps, general assembly. Sliding / running +0.30 to +0.40 mm Moves freely, small play. Hinge pins, drawers, rotating knobs. Loose +0.40 to +0.60 mm Obvious play, tolerant of warping. Large parts, hot-chamber materials, lids that must always close. Print-in-place 0.30–0.50 mm per side Parts print separated and move after printing. Chains, hinges, captive balls, gear trains. Figure 3. Hole-and-shaft sections for the fit classes (gaps exaggerated). The press fit is drawn with the shaft filling the hole entirely to show that, after printing, the shaft is slightly bigger than the undersized hole. Print-in-place clearances When two moving parts print together in one job, the gap between them must be large enough that the neighboring surfaces do not fuse, yet small enough to avoid slop. Horizontal gaps (side faces) and vertical gaps (top and bottom faces) behave differently because vertical gaps are quantized by layer height: each gap should be a multiple of the layer height, and at least two layers. Figure 4. A captive core inside a print-in-place sleeve. The vertical gaps must be multiples of the layer height; the side gaps must clear the squish-out of both parts. X2D note A hot chamber (up to 65 °C) keeps the plastic warmer and can reduce the effective gap, so print-in-place parts in ABS, ASA or nylon need 0.1 mm more side clearance than the same design in PLA with the chamber cold. Fans on the X2D also cool bridges and overhangs better; see Engineering materials & chamber . 🔧 Hole undersize rules, teardrops and diamonds Holes need two corrections: size (they print small) and shape (horizontal ones sag at the top, see Design principles ). First the size. Figure 5. Why mesh resolution matters for holes. A 16-sided polygon already makes a 10 mm hole 0.1 mm too small at the flats; use finely tessellated exports (or STEP files) for precision features. The second contribution is physical: the inner perimeter of a hole is pushed inward by the bead. The practical result is the following rule table. Horizontal, any size +0.25 to +0.40 mm Plus teardrop or diamond shape to avoid a sagging roof. Tiny holes < 2 mm +0.20 to +0.30 mm Often too tight; print undersize and drill. Screw clearance, M3 3.4–3.5 mm (nominal 3.0) Sl

x: Joints & fasteners · 3D Printing Compendium Part 5 · Design for printing Joints & fasteners Snap-fits that survive more than one use, nut traps that actually hold a nut, heat-set inserts, magnets, hinges, gears and every other way to hold printed parts together, with the dimensions that work on a 0.4 mm nozzle. Intermediate ⏱ 50 min read What you will learn How to choose between a snap-fit, a screw, an insert, a magnet and glue; how to size a cantilever snap-fit with simple beam math and a strain limit for your material; the pocket dimensions for M2–M8 nuts, heads and heat-set inserts; and the details that make hinges, bearings, gears and split parts go together. Clearances come from Tolerances & fits ; strength reasoning from Strength & orientation . Complete mechanisms built from these joints (hinges, latches, mounts, slides, clamps) are compared in the Mechanism catalog . 🔰 Choosing a joint Every joint is a trade between strength , reusability , assembly effort and extra hardware . Printing gives you geometry for free, so the cheapest joint is often one that needs no hardware at all (a snap-fit, a dovetail). The strongest and most reusable is usually a screw into a metal insert. Pick by asking three questions: how many times will it be opened , how big is the load , and in which direction does the load act relative to the layers . Figure 1. A quick map of joint choices. Start from the top (no hardware) and move down only when the load or the number of cycles demands it. Rule of thumb If it will be opened more than about five times, do not let plastic carry the thread or the latch alone. Use metal: an insert, a nut or a steel pin. If it will be opened once, print the latch and glue the rest. 🔧 Snap-fits A snap-fit stores elastic energy in a flexing arm, lets a hook ride over an undercut and then relaxes behind it. Done well, it replaces screws. Done badly, it breaks the first time you use it, because plastic that is bent beyond its elastic strain limit cracks, and printed parts have lower limits than the datasheet suggests (layer lines act as built-in notches). Three families matter: cantilever , annular and torsional . Cantilever snap-fit: the beam math A cantilever snap is a beam fixed at one end with a hook on the other. For a beam of constant rectangular section, length L , thickness h (in the bending direction) and width b , pushed aside by a deflection y (the undercut depth): ε max = 1.5 · h · y / L² (strain at the root, as a fraction; ×100 for %) P = E · b · h² · ε / (6 · L) (force needed to deflect the tip by y) Two things stand out. Strain grows with h and y but falls with the square of L : lengthening the arm by 50 % cuts strain by more than half. And force grows with h², so a thin, long arm is both gentle and safe. Figure 2. Cantilever snap-fit anatomy and the two formulas you need. Dimensions are in mm. Strain limits by material The permissible strain is the number that decides whether the design works. The values below are conservative design numbers for printed parts with layers running along the beam, not datasheet elongation. They are indicative: test one prototype before you commit to a design. Material One-off assembly (ε max) Repeated use (ε max) Comment PLA 0.8–1.0 % 0.4 % Stiff and brittle; long, thin arms only. Fatigues quickly. PETG 2.0 % 1.0 % The best everyday snap-fit material. ABS / ASA 1.8 % 0.9 % Good if layer adhesion is good (warm chamber). PC 2.5 % 1.2 % Tough but notch-sensitive; use big fillets. Nylon (PA, dry) 3.0–4.0 % 1.5–2.0 % Excellent fatigue; absorbs moisture and softens. PP 4.0 % 2.0 % Great for hinges and latches; difficult to print. CF/GF-filled 0.5–1.0 % 0.3–0.5 % Stiffer, strain-limited: needs longer arms than unfilled. TPU 95A 5–8 % 3–5 % Behaves like a spring; a snap arm may be unnecessary. Print orientation decides everything A snap arm must be printed so that the tensile stress runs along the extrusion lines, not across layers . A tall hook standing on its tip, bending sideways, will peel apart at a layer line at a fraction of the strain in the table. Figure 3. The same arm, two orientations. If the snap must stand upright, make it 2–3 times thicker or choose a different joint. Make the arm better: taper and fillet Strain peaks at the root of the arm. Two cheap changes lower it dramatically. Taper the thickness from h at the root to h/2 at the tip: strain follows ε ≈ 0.92 · h · y / L² , which allows about 64 % more deflection for the same peak strain. And add a root fillet of at least 0.5 × h (1 mm minimum) so the stress is not concentrated in a sharp corner. Many failed snaps broke at a 90° corner at the root, not in the middle of the arm. Figure 4. Three ways to shape a snap arm. Combine taper and fillet for the longest life. Hook geometry: how the angles set force The hook has two faces. The lead-in (insertion) ramp sets how hard it is to push in; the return face sets how hard it is to pull out. A ramp at 30°–45° from the motion direction lets the part snap in with moderate force. A return face at 90° is a permanent lock; at 45°–60° it releases when you pull. Keep the undercut y at 0.5–1.2 mm and the hook head at least 1.6 mm (four lines) wide, or the tip will print as a fuzzy sliver. Return face angle Behavior Use 90° (flat) Permanent, breaks before it releases Single-use closures, boxes you never reopen 60–75° Releases with a firm pull Battery doors, rarely opened lids 45° Releases easily; may pop loose under vibration Frequently opened lids, clips 30° Friction catch only Light detent, positioning Annular snap-fit An annular snap-fit is a ring that stretches over a bead: bottle caps, pen caps, round lids. The strain is the hoop (circumferential) strain: ε ≈ y / r , where y is the radial undercut and r the radius of the bead. A 20 mm diameter bead (r = 10 mm) with y = 0.2 mm gives 2 %: borderline for PETG, impossible for PLA. A ring is much stiffer than a beam, so cut 4–6 slits through the wall to turn it into separate cantilevers a
