All levels Includes X2D + AMS 2 Pro ⏱ Browse as needed How to use this page Type a keyword (for example stringing , PETG , aux nozzle ) in the search box, or tap a topic chip to narrow the list. Click a question to open the answer. Answers are deliberately short; follow the links for the full explanation. Numbers are typical starting points, not guarantees. Always check your material maker's datasheet and your printer's official documentation. Figure 1. The maker's journey and where each FAQ topic fits. All 🚀 Getting started 🧵 Materials 💻 Slicing 🔍 Quality ⚙️ Mechanical 📐 Design 🦺 Safety 🛒 Buying 🖨️ X2D & AMS 2 Pro 🎨 Multi-color 🧽 Post-processing 💰 Costs & business Expand all Collapse all Reset filters No question matches your search. Try a shorter keyword, or use the glossary and the site search (press / ). 🚀 Getting started What is 3D printing, in one paragraph? 3D printing (additive manufacturing) builds an object by adding material layer by layer from a digital model, instead of cutting it out of a block. The most common hobby type is FDM (fused deposition modeling): a hot nozzle melts plastic filament and draws each layer on a bed. Resin printers cure liquid with light, and industrial machines sinter powder or melt metal. See What is 3D printing? and Printing processes compared . Do I need CAD skills to start? No. Millions of ready-made models can be downloaded and printed as they are, and slicers let you scale, cut and combine them. CAD becomes useful when you want a custom bracket, a replacement part or a fitting that does not exist yet. Start with a beginner-friendly tool and move on later; see CAD & modeling software . What do I need besides the printer? Filament, a slicer, a flush cutter, a scraper or spatula, a small hex key set, a pair of calipers (they pay for themselves quickly), isopropyl alcohol for the build plate, and a dry place to store spools. Gloves and eye protection are good for post-processing. A realistic list by budget tier is on the resources page . How much does it cost to get started? Entry-level printers cost a few hundred dollars; capable enclosed, multi-color machines cost roughly four to six times more, and prices change often. Budget an extra 10-20% for filament, spare nozzles, a plate and tools. Running costs are small: a kilogram of common PLA costs around the price of a pizza, and typical parts use a few dozen grams. See Economics, licensing & sustainability . How long does a print take? A small part (a clip, a coin-sized token) can finish in 10-30 minutes. A phone stand is usually 1-3 hours, a helmet or a large enclosure can take a day or more. Time scales roughly with volume of plastic and inversely with layer height: halving the layer height roughly doubles the time. The slicer's estimate is usually within about 10-20% on a well-tuned printer. Which file formats do printers use? You download or export a mesh ( STL , 3MF , OBJ ) or a CAD solid ( STEP ), the slicer turns it into G-code, and the printer runs the G-code. 3MF is preferable to STL because it carries units, colors and slicer settings. Details in File formats & mesh repair . Where can I find models to print? Large public repositories exist, run by printer makers, open communities and commercial designers. Check the license on every model before selling prints. A curated list is in Resources , and licensing basics are in Economics & ethics . What should my first print be? Choose something small, flat-bottomed and useful: a cable clip, a coaster, a simple box. A calibration cube is fine but boring; a small boat-shaped torture test is good once the basics work. Use the manufacturer's recommended PLA and the stock profile. Walk through it in Your first print . Is FDM or resin better for a beginner? FDM is the safer, cheaper, lower-mess starting point and covers most functional work. Resin gives much finer detail for miniatures and jewelry, but needs gloves, ventilation, washing, curing and careful disposal. Many people run both eventually. See Printing processes compared . How steep is the learning curve today? Much gentler than a decade ago. Modern enclosed machines with auto-leveling and good default profiles produce good prints on day one. Mastering materials, tolerances and design for printing still takes months of practice, which is why this compendium has leveled exercises . What does "slicing" mean and why can't I just press print on an STL? The printer needs instructions, not a shape. The slicer cuts the model into layers and plans every extrusion path, speed, temperature and fan setting. Some printers appear to print "directly" because a cloud service or an app runs the slicer for you. Read Slicers compared . 🧵 Materials PLA, PETG, ABS: which should I use? PLA is the easiest and stiffest, ideal for display and indoor parts. PETG is tougher and handles more heat and moisture; it strings more. ABS and ASA resist heat (roughly 90-100 °C) and are good for functional parts but warp and need an enclosure and ventilation. When in doubt, begin with PLA and move on when you hit a concrete limit. The full comparison is in Filament overview and the material picker . Do I really have to dry filament? Most filament absorbs moisture from air. Wet plastic pops and hisses, leaves strings and rough surfaces and weakens parts. Nylon, TPU, PVA and PETG are most sensitive; PLA often tolerates a long time. Dry spools before they misbehave, store them sealed with desiccant, and follow the temperature on the manufacturer's label. See Drying & storage . How do I know filament is wet? Typical signs: crackling or popping at the nozzle, steam or bubbles, fine hairs between features, a dull or rough surface and brittle filament that snaps when bent. I

x: Applications & project ideas · 3D Printing Compendium Part 9 · Reference Applications & project ideas 3D printing is a manufacturing method, not a single product, so its uses are as varied as the people who own printers. This page tours twenty application areas with their real-world constraints, then gives you more than sixty project ideas by skill level, a few worked scenarios and an honest look at selling prints and where the technology may go. Beginner Intermediate ⏱ 35 min read What you will learn Where 3D printing beats traditional manufacturing and where it does not. For twenty application areas: what matters in practice, which materials usually fit, and what to watch when printing. Over sixty project ideas ordered by difficulty, plus how to turn a hobby into small-scale income without illusions. How to read industry news about the technology with healthy skepticism. Why people print: the sweet spot 🔰 Beginner · What 3D printing is good at Every manufacturing method has a sweet spot. Injection molding makes a million identical parts cheaply but needs an expensive steel tool first. CNC machining makes precise metal parts but wastes material. 3D printing needs no tooling, so the cost of the first part and the hundredth different part is almost the same. That gives it four main strengths: Customization: every part can be different at no extra setup cost (a handle that fits your hand, a bracket for your odd wall). Complexity: internal channels, lattices and merged assemblies cost no more than simple blocks, within the limits of the process. Speed to first part: from idea to object in hours, which makes iteration cheap. Distributed production: a printer in a school, a shop or a remote station can make what is needed on site. Its weaknesses are equally real: slow production, material properties that vary with orientation, rougher surfaces than molded parts, limited material choice at consumer level, and cost per part that does not fall much with volume. Good applications use the strengths and avoid the weaknesses. Figure 1. The core economic logic, drawn qualitatively (not real data). Where the break-even sits depends on part size, material, tooling cost and whether the shape can be molded at all, but the shape of the curves explains why printing dominates prototypes and one-offs. 🔧 Intermediate · Risk and responsibility Not all applications carry the same consequences if a part fails. A printed desk-tidy that cracks is a nuisance; a printed bicycle part that cracks can injure someone. Before choosing material and settings, decide which zone your project lives in. This decides how much testing, documentation and professional involvement is appropriate. Figure 2. Risk zones. Most hobby printing sits in the green and yellow zones. The red zone is professional territory: standards, traceability and regulators apply, and a home printer alone is not enough. Read this before the medical, aerospace and food sections This page gives general overviews of regulated fields so you understand how the technology is used. It does not describe how to make medical devices, flight hardware, safety equipment or food-contact products, and it is not professional or legal advice. Where a failure could hurt someone, use certified parts. Twenty application areas Each block below gives the idea, then three short notes: Consider (real-world constraints), Materials (typical choices, see Filament overview ) and Printing (what to watch while slicing and printing). Material names are starting points; always check temperature and chemical exposure of the actual use. Area Typical volume Typical stakes Usual materials Prototyping 1-20 Low PLA, PETG, resin Functional parts 1-100 Medium PETG, ABS/ASA, nylon Jigs & fixtures 1-10 Medium PLA, PETG, nylon-CF Household repair 1 Medium PETG, ASA, TPU Tabletop & miniatures 10-500 Low Resin, PLA Cosplay & props 1-5 Low PLA, PETG, TPU Education 1-30 Low PLA Medical & dental varies High certified resins, powders, metals Aerospace & automotive varies High industrial polymers, metals Consumer products 10-10,000 Medium PLA, PETG, nylon Construction large High cement mixes, clay, polymer Application groups 1-10 1 · Prototyping and product development The original killer application. Designers print form models to judge size and ergonomics, fit models to check how parts assemble, and functional prototypes to test mechanisms before ordering tooling. A prototype that costs a few dollars and an afternoon lets you fail early, when mistakes are cheap. Consider: A printed prototype is not the final part: properties and surface differ. Say what question each prototype answers (looks, fit, function) and design the test around it. Materials: PLA for form and fit, PETG or ABS/ASA for moderately loaded function, resin for fine detail, flexible TPU for seals and grips. Printing: Print fast and coarse (0.28 mm layers, low infill) while iterating; switch to a finer, slower profile only for the final review model. Figure 3. The rapid-prototyping loop. The skill is not printing; it is changing one variable per loop and writing down what you learned, so that the fifth version is better for a reason. 2 · Functional end-use parts Brackets, clips, knobs, covers, gears, drone mounts and machine guards: parts that do a job in daily use. Printing shines for odd shapes, small quantities and replacement of discontinued parts. Consider: Loads, temperature, chemicals and UV decide the material. Parts are weakest between layers, so plan load direction (see Strength & orientation ). Add generous fillets and wall thickness. Materials: PETG and ASA for general use, nylon and nylon composites for wear and toughness, PC blends for heat, TPU for damping. Printing: More walls (3-5) before more infill, dry the filament, print slower for strength-critical parts and test one before making ten. 3 · Jigs, fixtures and workshop helpers A jig guides a tool (drill, saw, router), a fixture holds a workpiece. x: Economics, licensing & sustainability · 3D Printing Compendium Part 9 · Reference Economics, licensing & sustainability A printer turns plastic, electricity and your time into objects, and each of those has a price, an impact and sometimes a legal or ethical strings attached. This page builds a realistic cost model with worked examples, shows when printing beats buying, explains how to price prints for sale, and then covers the environment, licenses, dangerous objects, safety-critical parts, accessibility and the open community that makes the hobby possible. Intermediate ⏱ 30 min read What you will learn The seven real costs behind a print and how to calculate each of them. A simple test for "print it or buy it", and a method to price prints for sale. What actually creates waste in 3D printing, and what you can do about it. The basics of copyright, licenses and remixing, with the limits of this guide clearly marked. Why some things must never be printed, and where the hard lines are. Not legal, financial or engineering advice This page is general education. Laws on intellectual property, product liability, taxes, consumer protection and regulated objects differ by country and change over time. Prices, fees and electricity rates here are round illustrative numbers, not quotes. For decisions with real money or real risk, ask a qualified professional in your jurisdiction. The cost model: what one print really costs Most beginners count only the filament. That is the smallest honest number you can quote, and sometimes it is not even the biggest cost. A complete model has seven parts. Cost Formula Typical order of magnitude Notes 1 · Material grams used ÷ 1000 × price per kg $15–40 per kg for common filaments Include supports, brim and purge, not just the model weight shown in the slicer. 2 · Electricity average watts ÷ 1000 × hours × price per kWh cents per print for PLA Heated chambers and long high-temperature prints use noticeably more. 3 · Machine amortization purchase price ÷ expected printing hours × print hours often the largest hidden cost Include accessories; use realistic lifetime hours. 4 · Maintenance and wear nozzles, plates, belts, lubricants, filters per print hour cents to tens of cents per hour Hardened nozzles and abrasive filaments raise it. 5 · Failures (cost of 1–4) × failure rate 3–15% for a tuned hobby setup Higher for new materials, large flat parts and tricky designs. 6 · Labor minutes of hands-on time × hourly value often exceeds all of the above for sale items Includes design, slicing, plate swaps, support removal and messaging. 7 · Post-processing and packaging consumables + extra labor sanding paper, primer, inserts, boxes For painted or assembled items this can double the price. 🔰 Worked example 1 · A plain PLA part Assume a 120 g part that prints in 6 hours, filament at $20 per kg, electricity at $0.20 per kWh, an average draw of 150 W, a $1,000 machine expected to run about 2,000 printing hours, maintenance of about $0.05 per print hour and an 8% failure allowance. Material: 120 g ÷ 1000 × $20 = $2.40 Electricity: 0.15 kW × 6 h = 0.9 kWh × $0.20 = $0.18 Machine: $1,000 ÷ 2,000 h × 6 h = $3.00 Maintenance: 6 h × $0.05 = $0.30 Subtotal: $5.88; failure allowance 8% ≈ $0.47 Total (without your time): ≈ $6.35 The surprise is that the machine, not the filament, takes the largest slice. Electricity, which people worry about most, is a rounding error for PLA. Figure 1. Where the money goes for a small PLA part. Change the inputs (a cheaper machine, a longer lifetime, pricier filament) and the slices move, but the lesson stays: count more than the plastic. 🔰 Electricity in more detail Power draw is not constant. The heatbed and chamber heaters cycle, motors run, fans spin. Measure your own printer with a plug-in power meter for a few prints and use your average. As a reference, Bambu Lab's published figures for the X2D are about 250 W steady-state for PLA and about 550 W for PC at 25 °C ambient, with 7–8 W in standby (the machine's maximum is 1,600 W at 220 V during heat-up, which is not a typical average). Treat vendor figures as a starting point, since your enclosure temperature, room and material will change the result. Figure 2. Electricity matters mostly for long, hot prints. For a typical PLA job it stays well below the cost of the filament. 🔧 Machine amortization: the hidden driver Amortization spreads the purchase price over the hours you will actually print. The number of lifetime hours is a guess, and it changes the result strongly: a machine that earns its keep over 4,000 hours is half as expensive per hour as one that lasts 2,000. It also means idle machines are expensive machines . A $1,000 printer used 5 hours per week for 3 years has run only about 780 hours; its true cost per printed hour is much higher than for a printer busy every day. Figure 3. The same machine costs eight times as much per hour if it is barely used. Utilization is the lever for anyone who sells prints. 🔧 Worked example 2 · A multi-color print A 90 g model in four colors can generate more waste than part weight. If a color change needs a purge of, say, 5 g per change and the print has 60 changes, that is about 300 g of purge, more than three times the part. Slicer-reported "flush" and "waste" values show this. Modern tools, including purge into infill, purge into support, and printers that offer more than one nozzle or a tool-changer design, exist largely to attack this number (see Multi-color & multi-material ). The numbers here are invented for the arithmetic; read your own slicer's totals. Part: 90 g × $20 per kg = $1.80 Purge and tower: 300 g × $20 per kg = $6.00, more than the part itself Time rises too, since each change takes tens of seconds to minutes If purge dominates, reduce the number of color changes, merge similar colors, choose designs with color layers instead of scattered islands, and let the slicer use waste for infill where your quality target allows. 🚀 Worked exam

A healthy learning diet mixes all eight; relying on only one type (for example videos) leaves gaps. Model repositories Before you design, search: someone may already have solved your problem. Each site has its own community, search quality and license conventions, so read the license on every model (see licenses and IP ). Tips for good downloads Prefer models with photos of real prints and comments from people who printed them. Download the source (STEP, 3MF or native CAD) when it is offered; it is easier to modify than a mesh. See File formats & mesh repair . OrcaSlicer , an open-source fork with many tuning tools; the project lives on GitHub . PrusaSlicer , open source, from Prusa Research . UltiMaker Cura , open source, with a large plug-in ecosystem; see the Cura project . Comparison and settings: Slicers compared and Slicer settings explained . CAD and modeling Easy start Tinkercad , a free browser tool, is ideal for first designs and for children. Parametric CAD FreeCAD (open source), Onshape (browser-based, with free and paid plans) and Autodesk Fusion (check its current license terms for personal use). Code and meshes OpenSCAD for code-based parametric models, CadQuery for Python, and Blender for sculpting and organic shapes. See CAD & modeling software and the parametric workflow . Mesh and file tools MeshLab , an open-source mesh processing and repair tool. The repair functions inside your slicer and CAD tools are often enough for simple cases. Calculators and planning This site includes its own calculators for cost, flow, shrinkage, drying and time, the material picker and the visual lab . Your slicer's estimates for time and weight are the best planning source, and a kitchen scale or caliper is the best check on them.
